articles.title: Concurso Unificado terá provas neste fim de semana no Piauí | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos disputam 200 oportunidades em nove órgãos estaduais, com provas em Teresina, Parnaíba, Picos e Floriano.
articles.summary: Candidatos disputam 200 oportunidades em nove órgãos estaduais, com provas em Teresina, Parnaíba, Picos e Floriano.
articles.body:
Concurso Unificado terá provas neste fim de semana no Piauí; salários chegam a R$ 13,5 mil — Foto: Divulgação

Os candidatos inscritos no Concurso Público Unificado do Governo do Piauí farão as provas neste sábado (10) e domingo (11) em Teresina , Parnaíba , Picos e Floriano. O certame reúne nove órgãos da administração estadual e oferece 200 oportunidades, sendo 100 vagas para contratação imediata e 100 para formação de cadastro de reserva.

Os salários iniciais variam entre R$ 3.000,12 e R$ 13.536,01 , conforme o cargo pretendido.

Devido à prorrogação das inscrições até 7 de setembro, o Governo do Piauí também adiou a aplicação das provas do Concurso Público Unificado. Inicialmente previstas para setembro, as avaliações passaram a ser realizadas em outubro.

Além das provas objetiva e discursiva, alguns cargos exigem curso de formação, etapa de caráter eliminatório.

Agência de Defesa Agropecuária do Piauí (Adapi)

Agência de Regulação dos Serviços Públicos Delegados do Estado do Piauí (Agrespi)

Departamento Estadual de Trânsito do Piauí (Detran-PI)

Secretaria da Assistência Técnica e Defesa Agropecuária (Sada)

Secretaria da Agricultura Familiar (SAF)

Secretaria do Desenvolvimento e Assistência Social, Família e Combate à Fome (Sasc)

A Sasc concentra 30 vagas imediatas. Desse total:

20 são para agente socioeducativo, sendo 14 destinadas a homens e seis a mulheres;

Já a Fundação Antares oferece cinco vagas imediatas para o cargo de agente superior de serviços, na área de Jornalismo.

Manhã: provas para candidatos da Agrespi, Seplan, Setur e Fundação Antares

Tarde: prova para o cargo de analista de trânsito do Detran-PI

articles.title: Pedágio eletrônico começa na MT-020 e MT-326 na quarta (14) | G1
articles.standfirst: Carros de passeio pagam R$ 13,67 em cada ponto; motorista não precisa parar em cabine e tem opções de pagamento por tag, aplicativo ou site.
articles.summary: Carros de passeio pagam R$ 13,67 em cada ponto; motorista não precisa parar em cabine e tem opções de pagamento por tag, aplicativo ou site.
articles.body:
Pedágio será implantado no trecho da MT-020 e MT-326 entre Paranatinga, Campinápolis, Água Boa e Canarana. — Foto: CS Rodovias Rota

A cobrança de pedágio começa à meia-noite de quarta-feira (14) nas rodovias MT-020 e MT-326, entre Paranatinga , Campinápolis , Água Boa e Canarana , no Leste de Mato Grosso. Para carros de passeio, o valor será de R$ 13,67 em cada ponto de cobrança.

O pedágio será feito pelo sistema eletrônico free flow, que identifica a placa ou a tag do veículo sem a necessidade de parar em cabines ou passar por cancelas. Ao todo, são seis pontos de cobrança: cinco na MT-020, nos km 403, 464, 516, 597 e 640, e um na MT-326, no km 190.

A concessionária CS Rodovias Rota da Integração assumiu o trecho no fim de março e informou que já investiu mais de R$ 100 milhões na recuperação das rodovias, sinalização, veículos e equipamentos.

Depois de passar pelo ponto de cobrança, o motorista pode pagar de três formas:

Tag: o valor é cobrado automaticamente de empresas como Sem Parar, ConectCar, Veloe, Move Mais e Greenpass.

Aplicativo ou site: o motorista pode consultar as passagens e fazer o pagamento pelo aplicativo ou pelo site da concessionária.

Totens: o pagamento também pode ser feito nos equipamentos instalados nos Serviços de Atendimento aos Usuários (SAUs), nos km 472 e 638 da MT-020.

O valor do pedágio muda de acordo com o tipo de veículo. Em caso de dúvidas, a concessionária atende pelo telefone 0800 020 0326, de forma gratuita.

articles.title: Advogado Marcos Pires morre aos 71 anos em João Pessoa | G1
articles.standfirst: Marcos Pires estava internado em um hospital da capital e morreu nesta quarta-feira (7), vítima de câncer.
articles.summary: O advogado Marcos Pires faleceu nesta quarta-feira (7) em João Pessoa, após lutar contra um câncer; ele exerceu a profissão por 40 anos na Paraíba.
articles.body:
Morre aos 71 anos o advogado Marcos Pires, em João Pessoa — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

O advogado Marcos Pires morreu na tarde desta quarta-feira (7), aos de 71 anos. Ele estava internado em um hospital de João Pessoa e foi vítima de câncer.

Marcos Pires dos Anjos Pires Bezerra deixa esposa, dois filhos e netos. O velório está previsto para acontecer na quinta-feira (8), assim como o sepultamento no Parque das Acácias, na capital.

Filho da ex-vereadora de João Pessoa Creuza Pires e do empresário Adrião Pires Bezerra, Marcos Pires exerceu a advocacia por 40 anos.

Ao longo da carreira, recebeu homenagens pelo trabalho desenvolvido. Em 2008, recebeu a Medalha de Epitácio Pessoa, maior honraria concedida pela Assembleia Legislativa da Paraíba (ALPB).

articles.title: Maduro e esposa serão acusados de tortura, diz agência | G1
articles.standfirst: Reportagem da Reuters desta quarta-feira (7) afirma que um anúncio oficial deve ser feito nos próximos dias. Ex-ditador será julgado em 2027.
articles.summary: Reportagem da Reuters desta quarta-feira (7) afirma que um anúncio oficial deve ser feito nos próximos dias. Ex-ditador será julgado em 2027.
articles.body:
O ex-ditador da Venezuela , Nicolás Maduro , e a mulher dele, Cilia Flores, devem enfrentar novas acusações na Justiça dos Estados Unidos . A agência Reuters afirmou nesta quarta-feira (7) que os dois devem responder por suposta tortura de cidadãos americanos.

O caso foi revelado primeiro pela CNN norte-americana. Fontes ouvidas pela emissora afirmaram que procuradores de Nova York estão preparando as acusações para apresentar à Justiça. Um anúncio oficial deve acontecer nos próximos dias.

Segundo a reportagem, as acusações estão relacionadas a "prisões ilegais" de cidadãos dos Estados Unidos que estavam na Venezuela durante o governo Maduro. Outras pessoas envolvidas nas detenções também podem ser denunciadas.

Maduro e Cilia estão presos em uma penitenciária de Nova York, nos Estados Unidos, desde o início do ano. As forças militares americanas capturaram o casal em Caracas em 3 de janeiro.

O ex-ditador venezuelano enfrenta quatro acusações criminais, entre elas conspiração para o narcoterrorismo e conspiração para importação de cocaína. Se for condenado, ele pode ser sentenciado à prisão perpétua.

Em julho, um juiz federal determinou que Maduro e Cilia devem começar a ser julgados em 1º de junho de 2027 . A defesa do casal pede que o caso seja arquivado.

Desde a prisão do ex-ditador, a Venezuela é governada de forma interina por Delcy Rodríguez, que era vice-presidente do país. A nova líder se aproximou dos Estados Unidos e chegou a se reunir com Donald Trump em setembro.

articles.title: Alvo de protestos na Grécia, Rubio defende 'poder sem remorso' | G1
articles.standfirst: Rubio argumentou que a lealdade à própria nação não é egoísta. Em Atenas, centenas de manifestantes protestaram contra a Otan e a presença militar dos EUA em guerras globais.
articles.summary: Rubio argumentou que a lealdade à própria nação não é egoísta. Em Atenas, centenas de manifestantes protestaram contra a Otan e a presença militar dos EUA em guerras globais.
articles.body:
Secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio, discursa durante visita à Grécia — Foto: Mark Schiefelbein/Reuters

O secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, instou as nações ocidentais nesta quarta-feira a abraçarem os valores da Grécia Antiga de “heroísmo, honra e dever”, associando esses ideais à agenda “America First” (América Primeiro) do presidente Donald Trump.

“Hoje em dia, tornou-se moda acreditar que uma política externa esclarecida significa priorizar a comunidade global em detrimento do próprio povo”, disse Rubio a autoridades gregas, diplomatas e outros convidados.

Com as ruínas do Partenon ao fundo, ele argumentou que os homens da Grécia Antiga “sabiam que não havia nada de egoísta ou errado na lealdade à própria nação”.

Possível candidato à indicação republicana para suceder Trump em 2028, Rubio proferiu o discurso no Pnyx, onde outrora se reunia a assembleia de cidadãos da Atenas Antiga.

O discurso de Rubio ecoou o discurso do vice-presidente JD Vance na Conferência de Segurança de Munique, em fevereiro de 2025, que apresentou os desafios da Europa como um afastamento dos valores ocidentais compartilhados e gerou críticas dos líderes do continente.

Isso foi seguido pela Estratégia de Segurança Nacional de Trump, de novembro de 2025, que alertou que a Europa enfrentava o “apagamento da civilização” devido à migração e aos desafios à soberania nacional.

“Hoje, nos encontramos em uma encruzilhada, pois a próxima década e as decisões que tomarmos escreverão a história do próximo século”, disse Rubio. “O rumo que tomarmos determinará se o Ocidente manterá seu lugar à frente do mundo ou se resignará a um futuro de atrofia, servidão e declínio.”

“Sob o governo do presidente Trump, os Estados Unidos fizeram sua escolha”, acrescentou Rubio. “Optamos pela busca sem remorso do poder nacional.”

Rubio faz uma visita a três aliados europeus da Otan como parte de uma viagem que começou na Islândia. Na manhã desta quarta-feira, Rubio e seu homólogo grego reafirmaram os estreitos laços entre os EUA e a Grécia nas áreas de segurança, energia e comércio. Ele encerra a viagem com conversas com autoridades portuguesas na quinta-feira, em Lisboa.

Centenas de pessoas se reuniram em frente ao Parlamento grego, em Atenas, para condenar a visita de Marco Rubio. Os manifestantes criticaram o envolvimento dos EUA e da Otan em conflitos militares ao redor do mundo, como as guerras na Ucrânia e no Oriente Médio.

articles.title: Michigan woman reported as little as $39,960 in income; prosecutors say she hid $1.66 million linked to gambling and embezzlement
articles.summary: A Michigan woman admitted filing federal tax returns that understated her income by more than $1.6 million, with prosecutors saying the money included
articles.body: A Michigan woman admitted filing federal tax returns that understated her income by more than $1.6 million, with prosecutors saying the money included cash taken from her employer and gambling proceeds. According to the IRS, Erin Patti-Coveyou of Moran, Michigan, pleaded guilty to making a false statement on a federal income tax return and is due to be sentenced later this year. The case involves several years of tax filings and a separate agreement to repay more than $1.75 million that she embezzled from her employer. The Internal Revenue Service says the understatement of income left the government with a tax loss of $535,605. Patti-Coveyou now faces up to three years in federal prison.Tax returns reveal wide gaps between reported and actual incomeAccording to the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan, Patti-Coveyou failed to disclose $1,666,499.78 in income on federal individual tax returns filed between 2021 and 2024.The figures varied sharply from what was actually earned. In one example cited by prosecutors, she reported $353,055 in income on her 2022 return for the previous tax year. The government says her actual income was higher because she had received another $279,079.12 through cash embezzlement from her employer and gambling activity.As reported by the IRS, the discrepancies continued in later returns. Amounts reported as $39,960, $53,188 and $56,545 were, according to the case, substantially below the corresponding income figures of $424,882, $461,300 and $650,931.The tax loss reached more than $535,000By leaving income off her returns, Patti-Coveyou reduced the amount of federal tax she owed. Prosecutors put the resulting loss to the Internal Revenue Service at $535,605. She has agreed to pay that amount in full as restitution to the IRS. The restitution is separate from the money she agreed to repay to her former employer. Reportedly, the guilty plea concerns one count of making a false statement on a federal income tax return. Patti-Coveyou's sentence will be decided by Chief US District Judge Hala Y. Jarbou, with sentencing scheduled for later this year.The case goes beyond Patti-Covey’s unpaid tax liabilityThe tax filings were not the only financial issue addressed by prosecutors. Patti-Coveyou also agreed to repay $1,751,059 that she embezzled from her employer between 2021 and 2025.The government says some of the unreported income came from that activity, along with money associated with gambling. The case therefore covers two connected financial obligations: the tax liability arising from income that was not reported to the IRS and the substantially larger amount owed to the employer from the embezzlement. The investigation was conducted by IRS Criminal Investigation, the law enforcement arm of the Internal Revenue Service that investigates suspected financial crimes involving federal tax laws.IRS-CI's work extends beyond false tax returns. Its remit includes cases involving money laundering, public corruption, healthcare fraud, identity theft and other financial offences. It is the only federal law enforcement agency with investigative jurisdiction over violations of the Internal Revenue Code.Robert Kuszynski, acting special agent in charge of the IRS-CI Detroit Field Office, said, “Taxpayers thinking about participating in fraudulent tax schemes, including failing to report all forms of income, should stop in their tracks and simply look at the consequences of taking the next step.”The case now turns to sentencing and financial repaymentPatti-Coveyou has pleaded guilty, but she has not yet been sentenced. The maximum penalty for the offence is three years in federal prison. The final sentence will be imposed by Judge Jarbou after the court considers the case. Alongside any prison term, Patti-Coveyou faces the financial obligations already set out in the proceedings, including the $535,605 restitution to the IRS and the agreement to repay $1,751,059 to her former employer.Assistant US Attorney Chris O'Connor is prosecuting the case. The case serves as a federal tax prosecution built around a relatively simple point in the filings: income that prosecutors say should have appeared on the returns did not.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian students' American dream hits a $ 70,000 toll
articles.summary: The TOI correspondent from Washington: Not too long ago, MAGA boss Donald Trump said foreign graduates should leave American universities with a green
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: Not too long ago, MAGA boss Donald Trump said foreign graduates should leave American universities with a green card “as part of your diploma.” Forget the green card; on Wednesday, his administration, under pressure from the nativist MAGA base, proposed a $70,000 fee to let those graduates work in America.Under a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposal scheduled for publication Thursday, US universities and colleges would have to pay $70,000 for an F-1 student’s first participation in Optional Practical Training (OPT) and another $30,000 for a subsequent authorization, including the 24-month extension STEM graduates are eligible for. The maximum charge over the standard 36-month STEM OPT period would therefore be $100,000. The proposal is not yet in effect and is subject to public comment.The legal obligation to cough up $70k OPT fee would fall on the university or other SEVP-certified school, not directly on the student. But as per the proposal, USCIS will not approve the student’s work authorization without payment. DHS nevertheless says schools could recover the cost from students, employers or other sources, which would effectively mean the nominally “school-paid” fee could ultimately become a charge on the student.This makes the proposal potentially far more than an immigration-fee adjustment -- it could mean the end of inflow of foreign students who want to gain work experience in the US after their studies. OPT is routinely the first step into the American labor market for foreign graduates – including for the likes of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella and Google’s Sundar Pichai – before they seek an H-1B specialty-occupation visa. Roughly 418,000 students had OPT work authorization in 2024, more than a quarter of F-1 students.India is likely to feel the proposal disproportionately, considering it sent 363,019 students to US institutions in 2024-25 -- roughly 31% of all international students -- making it the largest source country. Indian participation in OPT reached 143,740, up 47% in one year. Almost half of Indian students were graduate students, and India’s students are heavily concentrated in computer science, mathematics and engineering. STEM graduates can remain in OPT for as long as three years.The new fee proposed by the Trump administration is not the end of foreign-student inflows -- students can still study in America without OPT and many who are ready to return to their home countries as soon as they complete studies will still come. But if universities -- many already under financial strain amid dwindling foreign admissions -- conclude that paying $70,000 per student is untenable, prospective students, especially those choosing expensive STEM graduate programs partly because they expect US work experience, may increasingly choose Canada, Britain, Australia or other destinations.The proposal comes as the administration argues that OPT has become a “back door” into the American workforce. DHS cites fraud, abusive worksites and “pay-to-stay” schemes and says the enormous fee would force schools to exercise greater scrutiny over employers and students. The administration’s broader immigration policy makes the rationale clear: it argues that foreign labor, particularly lower-paid labor supplied through outsourcing companies, can displace Americans and suppress wages.There is genuine evidence of abuse in parts of the temporary-worker system. The Labor Department’s inspector general has launched investigations into alleged H-1B fraud and wage-kickback schemes, while DOJ this year settled a case involving a company accused of improperly excluding US workers from jobs advertised for H-1B, OPT and H-4 workers.But the larger MAGA argument -- that foreign graduates are broadly unnecessary because Americans can fill these jobs -- is much harder to reconcile with the structure of the US STEM workforce. According to the National Science Foundation (NSF) 22% of America’s 36 million STEM workers were foreign-born in 2023. Among workers in science and engineering occupations, the foreign-born share is substantially higher at advanced degree levels. Temporary-visa holders earned 38% of US science-and-engineering master’s degrees and 39% of doctorates in 2023. India is particularly important: Indian-born workers accounted for more than 727,000 of America’s foreign-born S&E workforce.This does not prove that every OPT worker is indispensable -- or that every claimed shortage is real. Indeed, the STEM labor market is not uniformly tight. But it does demonstrate that the US does not currently produce all of the advanced STEM talent its research universities and technology industries consume.Ironically, it was not long ago that there was broad bipartisan enthusiasm for the US retaining foreign graduates, including from MAGA boss Donald Trump, whose administration is now tightening the screws on international students and foreign workers. Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton backed versions of the idea of effectively “stapling” green cards to advanced STEM degrees. Republican Presidential candidate Mitt Romney made a similar proposal in 2012. And Trump himself, in 2024, went considerably further, saying: “You graduate from a college, I think you should get automatically, as part of your diploma, a green card.” He explicitly included two- and four-year colleges and junior colleges.Silicon Valley too has long plugged for OPTs and H1Bs. Elon Musk publicly defended H-1Bs during a December 2024 clash with MAGA activists, saying the program was essential to recruiting talent. “Take a big step back and F**K YOURSELF in the face. I will go to war on this issue the likes of which you cannot possibly comprehend," Musk raged as MAGA nativists drummed up a campaign against H1Bs and OPTs. The fight exposed a fundamental tension inside Trump’s coalition: nationalist immigration restriction versus the technology industry’s demand for global talent. Musk has since been far less publicly prominent as an advocate for H-1B expansion, while Trump himself has been tamed and tutored on the issue by nativist MAGA hardliners.For Indian students in particular, the message is stark: America may still welcome you into its universities, but the administration is proposing to make the transition from classroom to US workplace very expensive. Whether that protects American workers or drives some of the very talent America has spent years and billions of dollars educating to its competitors will be the central question of the coming years.You use AI every day. articles.title: State seeks Rs 11,000 crore central aid as drought losses mount
articles.summary: Karnataka seeks Rs 11,000 crore central drought aid as losses hit Rs 46,000 crore; 217 taluks declared drought-hit, farmers report crop failures and pending insurance claims.
articles.body: Ballari: Karnataka has sought Rs 11,000 crore in drought relief from the Centre against an estimated loss of Rs 46,000 crore, deputy chief minister G Parameshwara said during his visit to drought-hit Halakundi village in Ballari taluk on Wednesday.Reviewing crop damage in the village, he said the state is facing its worst drought in 75 years. “The govt has already declared 217 taluks as drought-hit and will add more taluks to the list in the coming days,” he said.Parameshwara said prolonged rain deficit has dried up crops, causing heavy losses to farmers. During his interaction with them, he heard accounts of crop damage and the hardships they continue to face.Farmer Durganna said he had spent about Rs 45,000 cultivating tur on three acres. With adequate rainfall, the fields were expected to yield 5-6 quintals per acre. However, the rain deficit destroyed the crop, leaving him with no yield and substantial losses. Farmers urged the govt to assess the damage and provide adequate compensation. They said the Rs 2,500 relief announced by the govt was insufficient and pointed out that crop insurance claims were yet to be settled despite premiums being paid.Parameshwara said the Centre would provide Rs 8,500 per hectare as drought relief, while the state govt would add Rs 2,500. “We will not allow farmers to die by suicide,” he said.He added that the central drought assessment team may not be able to visit every taluk as it had already obtained satellite data, and the state govt had also presented the drought situation before the team. articles.title: Over 100 arrested in Belgium student protests over education costs
articles.summary: Protesting students have demanded education reforms in French-speaking areas of the country.
articles.body:
Police in Belgium have detained more than 100 people after demonstrations in the city of Liege against the rising cost of education turned violent in some places, as similar protests grip neighbouring France.

Students rallied in the city on Tuesday and Wednesday against overcrowded classrooms and difficulty accessing resources in Belgium’s French-language education system.

Eighty people were detained during the protests, and 27 were formally arrested, the Belga news agency reported, citing the Liege police.

Some protesters damaged property and set fires, the police added.

Attendees insisted that shortcomings in the education system gave them no choice but to take to the streets.

“When we saw nothing was changing without protests, we decided we would start,” said Amelia Di Salve, a 19-year-old studying to become a teacher, who added that protests in “France did influence us a little”.

“We support each other because we’re facing pretty much the same issues,” Alfred, another 19-year-old ⁠student, told the Reuters news agency.

Authorities were attempting to defuse tensions and head off further unrest.

“Dialogue can be established,” Willy Demeyer, the mayor of the city of Liege, told Belgian broadcaster RTBF, adding that he hoped “young people can express their grievances in a peaceful way and if possible have those concerns heard”.

In Belgium, education is managed independently by the country’s linguistic communities, and there is no single national curriculum.

Instead, the Flemish population regulates education in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking Flanders region while French-speaking Wallonia oversees its own curriculum.

Parents can decide where to enrol children in the bilingual capital Brussels.

The protests in Liege follow sporadic violent demonstrations over the summer in Brussels against an increase in tuition fees for students in French-speaking areas from 835 euros ($930) to 1,194 euros ($1,340).

Belgium’s education budget has been under pressure as a result of a cost-of-living crisis and the spiralling cost of energy, issues that are helping fuel student protests in France as well.

articles.title: Researchers coated a brick bungalow roof with a self-cleaning, heat-radiating material; the roof was 3.4°C below outdoor air and the room reached 10.2°C below the control
articles.summary: Discover how researchers in China developed a game-changing self-cleaning, heat-radiating coating that can drastically cool homes and buildings, achieving indoor temperatures significantly lower than the ambient air.
articles.body: Researchers testing a highly emissive coating on a brick bungalow in rural China recorded a roof surface temperature 3.4°C below outdoor air and an indoor drop of 10.2°C versus the control, according to a study at Renmin University of China. The superomniphobic, self-cleaning, highly emissive (SSC-HE) coating was engineered to reflect solar energy while emitting heat as infrared radiation. It achieved a 0.985 solar reflectance and an emissivity of 0.991 within the 8–14 micrometre atmospheric transparency window.The experiment was part of a more extensive research study examining whether the coating could provide cooling below ambient temperature, while dissipating heat from the equipment and improving heater performance. Additional testing included insulated silos, metal containers and a telecommunications base station.Cooling a brick bungalow below outdoor airTwo single-story brick buildings in Dengzhou City, Henan Province, hosted the bungalow experiment, and each measured 12 metres long, 5.5 metres wide and 3 metres high. The buildings were also constructed with 24-centimetre brick walls and 20-centimetre prefabricated concrete roofs, and throughout the testing phase, both rooms remained completely closed. For comparison, the roof and walls of one building was coated with SSC-HE, while the control building had common white-coated walls and an unpainted concrete roof..In early autumn 2023, the coated roof stayed below ambient air temperature across five consecutive sunny days, while the control roof became much hotter. On September 1, when the outdoor air reached 37.7°C, the SSC-HE-coated roof reached 34.3°C, which was 3.4°C and 40.8°C below the ambient air and control roof temperatures, respectively.This difference in temperatures extended indoors, as on the same day the SSC-HE-coated bungalow's room reached 26.6°C, compared to the 36.8°C in the control. The room was 10.2°C cooler than the control and 11.1°C below outdoor ambient air, and for the next four days its maximum temperature remained below 28°C.Beyond a single test, the material kept working Another test examined a distributed telecommunications base station in Ziyang, Sichuan Province where the HE primer and SSC topcoat were applied to the base station and temperatures were recorded after one month and again after one year. During clear, sunny conditions, the battery cabinet remained below ambient temperatures andthe sub-ambient cooling effect reached 5.3°C in September 2021 and 5.1°C in August 2022 . Furthermore, the coating’s emissivity also influenced the heat dissipation indoors, as water in the coated tank cooled from 58.7°C to 20.7°C, whereas the control tank fell from 58.9°C to 27.7°C, leaving a 7°C difference. Water in the coated tank, under adiabatic conditions, cooled from 88.8°C to 34.8°C, ending 12.4°C below the control.Researchers also tested the HE coating on electric oil heaters in early 2024 at identical room-temperature settings. The coated heater used 0.4 kWh less energy than the heater coated with aluminium, corresponding to 5.9% heating energy efficiency. Against a black-coated heater, it used 0.4 kWh less energy and achieved the equilibrium room temperature 111 minutes faster, reflecting a heating energy efficiency of 4.4%. At similar power consumption, rooms heated by the HE-coated heater reached equilibrium temperatures 2.1°C and 1.9°C higher than those heated with aluminium coating and black coating respectively.The coating was tested on galvanised steel silos, including one with 10-centimetre-thick polyurethane (PU) insulation. On May 31, 2024, when ambient air reached 34.3°C, the coating lowered the interior air temperature of the PU-insulated silo by as much as 6.9°C compared with the uncoated insulated silo. The coating also outperformed other cooling approaches; in a separate test on a chemical pipeline in Yinchuan, it measured 34°C, in contrast to an unpainted pipeline protected by a sunshade and continuously sprayed with water, which measured 41°C. Overall, results indicated that the coating's high solar reflectance and emissivity affected cooling, heat dissipation and heating performance across the tested structures and equipment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Former CIA officer warns against trusting Russia's account of mysterious death in Siberia
articles.summary: Glenn Corn, a former CIA officer, explains why Vladimir Putin's Kremlin cannot be trusted on the Russian researcher's death, citing past coverups.
articles.body: Glenn Corn, a former CIA officer, told Fox News Digital that Russia’s decades-long history of deception makes it difficult to trust the Kremlin’s account of a possible disease outbreak following the death of a 28-year-old researcher at a facility containing dangerous pathogens. Darya Shipilova, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, got sick near the end of September. After unconfirmed reports that Shipilova died from pneumonic plague were shared far and wide on social media, Russian authorities pushed back, saying she died on Oct. 2 from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing found no evidence she had been infected with a pathogen from her lab. Yet the Russian government’s past messaging around major crises has left Corn and others wary of its official account. RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS "This is what the challenge is, because they have the history of the 'boy who cried wolf syndrome.' They have this history of being deceitful. It's very hard to believe what they're saying," said Corn, a professor at the Institute of World Politics, a graduate school in Washington, D.C. Corn, who is fluent in Russian and spent more than 20 years overseas during his intelligence career, gave several examples of elaborate Russian coverups, including the 1979 anthrax outbreak that killed at least 64 people in the Soviet city of Sverdlovsk, now called Yekaterinburg. For years, the Soviet Union claimed that the deaths were caused by intestinal anthrax from tainted meat, according to PBS' "Frontline." It wasn't until 1992 that President Boris Yeltsin finally admitted the illnesses were the result of military activity at a nearby biological weapons facility. This dedication to deception, Corn said, remains a feature of the current government under President Vladimir Putin. AMB. GORDON SONDLAND: THE GODFATHER TEST -- HOW PUTIN TURNS EVERY ATTACK INTO A MYSTERY—AND GETS AWAY WITH IT Corn pointed to the Kremlin’s past denials of ties to the Wagner mercenary group, whose murky relationship with the state allowed its fighters to advance Moscow’s interests overseas while Russian officials maintained plausible deniability. Putin later acknowledged that the group had been fully financed by the Russian state. "This goes to the strategic culture of leadership in Russia... and their fear of the rest of the world, and their belief that they have to deceive everybody because everybody is deceiving them," Corn said. Corn said this style of narrative control is also characteristic of China, which remains under Communist Party rule, while modern Russia inherited many of the institutions and governing practices of the communist-led Soviet Union. For example, China faced criticism in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic for withholding or delaying the release of critical information about the emerging virus, which has gone on to kill more than 7 million people globally. TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR "In both systems, people are disincentivized to tell the truth when there's a bad story," Corn said. "Nobody wants to actually say that we have a real problem and we need to deal with it because they're afraid that it will cost them their jobs, their lives, their freedom." With that history in mind, Corn said U.S. officials should not simply take Moscow at its word on Shipilova’s death, but independently verify its claims and closely monitor for any signs of a wider outbreak. So far, there is no sign that Shipilova’s illness has spread. Russia's health watchdog said Tuesday that 60% of the roughly 200 people quarantined after potentially coming in contact with Shipilova have been released. It added that no cases of plague have been found. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday that the case presented a "very low" risk outside Russia, The Associated Press reported. That same day, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on social media that the global health agency is in contact with Russian health authorities and has requested more information "to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia" that killed Shipilova. President Donald Trump also told reporters on Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Putin about the case "very soon," adding that the U.S. is already in "very deep discussions" with Russia.

articles.title: IIT-Bombay puts tougher penalties for cheating on hold, students can have their say on form
articles.summary: IIT Bombay pauses stricter cheating penalties, reverts to 2015 rules for Oct 10-11 exams; interim SOP lets faculty log suspects and students submit accounts.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Putting its July 2026 rules on penalties for academic misconduct on hold and reverting to the (milder) April 2015 policy for two pending mid-semester examinations on Oct 10 and 11, IIT-Bombay’s senate, at its emergency meeting on Wednesday, agreed on an interim procedure under which faculty members may record suspected dishonesty by a student in a prescribed form, with students allowed to submit their own written accounts in a different sheet.The revision comes in the wake of the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode, who was allegedly found copying by an invigilator. The institute subsequently postponed exams scheduled for Sept 26 and 27 after faculty sought a clear SOP for handling suspected malpractice.According to the interim arrangement now finalised, there will be two different forms in the event of a suspected case of cheating, and it is optional for the student concerned to submit their version. The matter will then be placed before the departmental disciplinary action committee (DDAC), which will decide how the case proceeds. Faculty members and students will be required to appear before the committee and provide additional information as needed. The committee will meet only a week after the entire exam season ends.A source said the forms were only a means of collecting information and did not amount to pressing charges. Decisions would rest with the disciplinary committee.Wednesday’s meeting was opened to all faculty, beyond the senate’s membership, to seek suggestions.The report on the interim rules, a copy of which is with TOI, states faculty who suspect cheating or notice signs of stress must “alert a quick response team (QRT) of counsellors.” The aim is to provide immediate support “while minimising disturbance to the student concerned and others writing the examination.”Invigilators, the report states, must “collect unauthorised material, including chits, phones, devices and answer papers, with minimal conversation and disruption. They may photograph material that must be returned, such as a phone. If a student’s identity is in doubt, they may photograph the student at the desk.”The original answer book will be collected and the student allowed to continue writing in a fresh one for the remaining exam time. After the exam, the invigilator may complete the form and offer the student an opportunity to record their account at a designated venue in the presence of additional staff, said the report.The signed faculty form, collected material, original answer book and student’s form, if submitted, will be handed to the head of the department conducting the course. “Digital material may be emailed. Phones must be returned after the examination, with students acknowledging receipt by signing the form.” The QRT helpline must be alerted for counselling whenever the student leaves the hall.Under the 2015 guidelines, using a mobile phone during an exam attracted an FR (fail-repeat) grade. The July 2026 policy added a semester’s suspension, which sources said would not apply to a first offence under the interim arrangement. Repeat offences would attract suspension. Using phones, chits, books or other unauthorised material during toilet or bio-breaks would continue to attract FR and a semester’s suspension.Security guards will no longer frisk students before exams. Faculty questioned searches resembling those at airports, saying they suggested everyone was a “suspect”.“We want to convey we trust our students, though we will verify by doing thorough invigilation,” said a faculty member. Another source said an invigilator who suspected something could call a counsellor and ask the student to empty pockets.The report states disciplinary proceedings must ensure students have a fair opportunity to present their viewpoints to the departmental committee and provide an appeal before an institute committee. Disciplinary action will follow if unauthorised practices are established.Sources said the arrangement would “ease the burden on faculty handling suspected cheating, with professional counsellors providing support.” The disciplinary committee, however, will determine the outcome.The drafting committee comprised Profs Suvarn Kulkarni, Pratibha Sharma, Varsha Apte and Amitava De and four student representatives. Sources said they spent about 30 hours preparing the interim procedure. Clear instructions would be shared with invigilators before the weekend exams, a source added.Students may now bring bags into the exam building, reversing the earlier restriction, but must leave them outside the hall. The report states the institute’s goal is to “create an environment conducive to quality teaching and learning while maintaining assessment integrity. Its default assumption is that students are committed to learning and following examination rules.”As per the academic calendar approved by the Senate, end semester examinations are scheduled for 13 days from November 10 to 21 and will be held on Saturdays and Sundays as well.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: ‘Don’t think it’s bioweapon’: Trump weighs in on mysterious Siberia lab death
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump said the United States does not believe the death of a laboratory worker in Siberia was caused by a bioweapon, but said
articles.body: US president Donald Trump said the United States does not believe the death of a laboratory worker in Siberia was caused by a bioweapon, but said Washington would investigate the circumstances surrounding the case.Trump also said Russia had told the US that the situation was under control.The death of the worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East has raised concerns because the facility specialises in studying plague. Russia has said the woman died of pneumonia and that extensive testing found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with.However, the World Health Organisation has said it still does not know what caused the woman's illness and has asked Russia for more information. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the agency did not know the “causative agent” behind the woman's death and added, “this is why we need more information”.Russian authorities have said no cases of plague have recently been registered in the Irkutsk region. They have also reported contact tracing, medical monitoring and laboratory testing, with no dangerous infectious pathogens detected among the contacts.The case has nevertheless drawn international attention amid reports that the worker developed severe pneumonia before dying on October 2. A hospital where she was treated was placed under quarantine, while people who had contact with her were monitored.The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has described the risk to Americans as extremely low, while saying it is prepared to monitor travellers arriving from the region.The WHO has continued to seek clarity on the cause of the illness, the pathogen involved and reports of another employee developing pneumonia of unknown origin.You use AI every day. articles.title: Norwich schoolgirl was stabbed by masked 15-year-old, court hears
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the boy had an "intention to kill" a 15-year-old girl.
articles.body:
A masked 15-year-old who was captured on CCTV stabbing a schoolgirl had written notes saying he hated women, a court has heard.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder - but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

The boy brought a knife to school, dressed in black with a face mask and had an "intention to kill", prosecutors told King's Lynn Crown Court.

Police were called to reports of the stabbing at 10:24 GMT, not long after parents had gathered at the gates.

Opening the prosecution case, Chris Paxton KC said the defendant armed himself with a kitchen knife and "went to school not to learn, but to kill".

He was "dressed in black, masked up and tooled up", jurors heard.

CCTV footage shown to the court captured the moment the girl was stabbed in the back, before her attacker ran off while "pursued by a teacher".

The girl was treated in hospital for minor injuries and later discharged.

Her alleged attacker was said to have written down his motive as "misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying".

His notes continued: "Death = 2+ hopefully, injuries a lot hopefully."

The prosecution described it as "sheer good fortune" that the girl was not seriously hurt and said she had been "defenceless and vulnerable".

"This was a knife strike delivered, we the prosecution say, as an attempt to kill," Paxton added.

A search of the defendant's house revealed evidence of his "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", it was alleged.

Jurors heard about notes found by police which said "I really want to do it really bad", adding: "I need a plan."

Paxton said further notes - including one called "victims list" - displayed a hatred of women.

The trial, which is expected to last three weeks, continues.

articles.title: US shelves Sudan arms embargo proposal amid UN Security Council divisions
articles.summary: The Trump administration is shelving its proposal for an arms embargo on Sudan amid divisions on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), which will instead vote Thursday on a short-term extension of a more regional arms embargo that would just impact Darfur. The vote on UNSC Resolution 1591 would extend the Darfur arms embargo until…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is shelving its proposal for an arms embargo on Sudan amid divisions on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), which will instead vote Thursday on a short-term extension of a more regional arms embargo that would just impact Darfur.

The vote on UNSC Resolution 1591 would extend the Darfur arms embargo until Dec. 11, according to a draft of the resolution obtained by The Hill.

The draft resolution is proposed by the U.S., which holds authority for drafting text related to Sudan sanctions, the so-called penholder.

The vote on the extension was confirmed by Sudan’s deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, Ammar Mohammed Mahmoud.

“Sudan welcomes the Security Council’s decision to technically renew the measures under resolution 1591 for sixty days without expanding their geographic scope. Sudan has consistently maintained that the priority should be to enforce the existing sanctions regime, not expand it,” Mahmoud said in a statement to The Hill.

The vote for a short-term extension underscores the deep divisions on the Security Council over the U.S. proposal to expand the arms embargo to the entire country.

While the arms embargo has failed to halt weapons flows, 1591’s reporting requirements are viewed as an important tool in documenting the networks facilitating arms transfers and recommending individuals and entities for sanctions. The U.S. draft resolution extends the mandate for the Panel of Experts — an independent UNSC body established to monitor the implementation of sanctions — until Jan. 11.

The expanded arms embargo was initially proposed in August by Massad Boulos, President Trump’s point person on peace negotiations for Sudan. The county is embroiled in a devastating three-year civil war that has been one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The fighting is centered around rival generals: Gen. Abdel-Fattah Burhan, the head of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF); and his former deputy, Gen. Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo, the head of paramilitary group the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Both sides are accused of war crimes, although U.N. experts and the U.S. have accused the RSF of carrying out genocide. The fighting is further complicated by the participation of approximately 150 militias on the ground, and a constellation of external backers to the SAF and RSF.

Boulos, backed by U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz, sought to use a more than two-decade old arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region — Resolution 1591 — to increase pressure on the SAF and RSF by expanding sanctions to the whole of the country.

“The United States has presented a resolution to the Security Council that would expand the arms embargo nationwide, making clear that sanctions and member state implementation of those rules apply to all the networks keeping this war alive—on both sides, with no carve-outs,” Boulos and Waltz wrote in an op-ed for Foreign Policy in September.

“Yes, it will even apply to the arms traffickers, procurement agents, mercenary recruiters, state-backed patrons, established financiers, drone suppliers, and genocidal commanders who have for so long evaded justice.”

But pushback from veto-wielding powers China and Russia — and a number of the nonpermanent members of the Security Council — have delayed the U.S. putting its proposal to a vote.

That opposition was on display in a vote in September, when the U.S. was forced to put forward a short-term one-month extension of 1591 to allow time for more negotiations on its expansion proposal.

Opponents of the U.S. proposal say it undermines the SAF, who they view as a legitimate institution of the Sudanese state, and draws a false equivalency with the genocidal RSF.

Mahmoud, in a statement to The Hill, said “the fundamental problem” with 1591 is that it has failed to stop weapons flows in Darfur, particularly to the RSF.

“A failure of enforcement cannot be remedied by expanding sanctions against the State suffering the consequences of those violations,” he said.

“Sudan therefore remains firmly opposed to extending the arms embargo nationwide. Such a measure would blur the fundamental distinction between Sudan’s legitimate national armed forces and militias and mercenaries operating outside State authority, while potentially weakening the State’s ability to protect its territory and population.”

The Trump administration rejects that the SAF — and Burhan — hold legitimate governing authority.

“Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan – they rule through force of arms alone” Tommy Pigott, the State Department’s spokesperson, said in a statement last month.

“The conduct of each leader of the warring factions renders them ineligible to govern the country. We seek to restore peace and give power back to the Sudanese people.”

articles.title: What to know about Kenya’s first Ebola case and how officials are responding
articles.summary: Kenya’s first Ebola case, a patient who travelled for weeks by road and air through three countries without being detected until he arrived in Nairobi, has raised questions about border control and how to trace the virus across countries.
articles.body: Kenya’s first Ebola case, a patient who travelled for weeks by road and air through three countries without being detected until he arrived in Nairobi, has raised questions about border control and how to trace the virus across countries. The patient, a Kenyan man, had been living in Congo for seven years and started feeling ill a month ago. He had traveled by road to Uganda before boarding a flight to the Kenyan capital on Saturday. There, he tested positive for the Ebola virus in a hospital and died Monday. The Africa CDC Director-General, Jean Kaseya, told The Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that all stakeholders need to ask themselves how one case could have driven and flown to so many places without anyone noticing. “We need to ensure that at point of entry, we have a strong surveillance system in place,” he said. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. Officials are trying to trace all who came into contact with the patient The Kenyan man drove for hours by road within Congo and across the border into Uganda. He boarded a local flight while in Congo, and it is unclear if he used any other forms of public transport. Authorities have looked at the flight manifest of the other flight he took from Kampala, Uganda, to Nairobi, and passengers and crew onboard have been added to the contact list. They’re also looking to trace workers who cleaned the plane after it landed, as well as passengers who traveled on the same plane subsequently. Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on Wednesday that contact tracing was ongoing and that the number of contacts had risen to 57, with 10 already quarantined. “Even the people who cleaned that aircraft after it landed on Saturday, they are part of the people we are tracing. The immigration and the customs officials who served that patient will also be part of the contact tracing,” he said. Africa CDC’s Kaseya acknowledged it is a challenge. He said that the Kenyan man had not come up in existing contact lists in Congo. “Before saying that the outbreak is under control, you need to ensure that you have a contact list where all cases are coming from,” he said. Questions raised about how the patient traveled through Uganda It’s also unclear how the patient was able to cross into Uganda, which has closed its border with Congo because of the Ebola outbreak. Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media center, dismissed the question, saying only that journalists should instead ask Kenya how the man was able to bypass surveillance at its airport. “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X. Two of the man’s journeys were by air, while the rest were by road, covering long distances and passing through various towns and cities. On arrival in Nairobi, the patient underwent port health screening but his symptoms were not detected. He then boarded a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated and later tested positive for Ebola. When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health, Patrick Amoth, said on Wednesday that a meeting was scheduled with officials from Congo and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate what transpired during the patient’s journey. Kenya has been boosting its border controls Kenya’s Health Ministry has heightened surveillance at border entry points and created an Ebola hotline for citizens to report symptoms related to Ebola. The country has also designated five health facilities with a total of 241 isolation beds to manage patients, and is working to increase this capacity. The ministry said the country has enough supplies, including personal protective equipment, and has mobilized resources since the outbreak started in May in Congo. The ministry added that it had designated a specific gate at the country’s main airport for passengers travelling from 10 countries located within the outbreak’s epicenter.

articles.title: Russia says no epidemic risk as WHO pushes for transparency on plague lab death
articles.summary: Russia’s health watchdog said Wednesday there is no risk of an epidemic following the death of a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Siberia, even as the World Health Organization made a plea for more information about the concerning episode.
articles.body: Russia’s health watchdog said Wednesday there is no risk of an epidemic following the death of a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Siberia, even as the World Health Organization (WHO) made a plea for more information about the concerning episode. In a statement Wednesday, Rospotrebnadzor said it is winding down a set of preventative measures in Russia’s Irkutsk region where the laboratory is located. Medical monitoring has been completed for “over 90%” of contacts of the deceased worker, and no dangerous pathogens have been found, it added. The death of the lab technician, who worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in Russia’s southeast, has sparked international concern and speculation in recent days about the cause of her illness. Russian authorities sought to alleviate those worries on Wednesday, with the country’s watchdog saying, “As of October 7, 2026, medical monitoring has been completed for over 90% of contacts. No health issues related to infectious disease were detected, and the results of nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.” Local authorities have previously introduced disease-control measures at local hospitals in Irkutsk, a move that fueled questions among some local residents about whether authorities were being transparent. Global health experts urge greater transparency But despite the positive statement from Russian authorities, global health experts are still urging caution, and asking for more transparency from Moscow. WHO chief Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that a “full risk assessment” has not been possible following the death of the Russian worker, adding that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” WHO’s experts also updated their early evaluation that the lab worker’s death posed “low” risk to public health, saying that because she may not have died of pneumonic plague — a bacterial infection that can be transmitted from person to person, but doesn’t spread easily — the risk from the event was now undetermined. Meanwhile, Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of the WHO’s department of epidemic and pandemic management, said the organization had reached out to colleagues in Russia’s Ministry of Health and expected “further answers.” “So we do reach out to them to ask very detailed questions about what tests were done, the results of those laboratory tests,” she said. “What further analysis is being done if the cause is not yet known, what contacts were put under quarantine or under follow up.” “What we have been told is that they had no case of plague registered in this area, and that no high-threat pathogens were detected,” Van Kerkhove said. “So clearly, we would like more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, and if this individual didn’t die from plague, then how did she die?” The Kremlin has dismissed the concerns and said that it has kept the WHO informed “in accordance with established practice.” Under its International Health Regulations, designed to prevent the cross-border spread of disease, WHO member states are obliged to notify it of “events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern.” US presses for more info The Trump administration is also struggling to get clear answers about the incident from Moscow, though Trump said Wednesday that the US does not believe that Shipilova died from exposure to a bioweapon, adding that the Kremlin has since insisted the situation at an anti-plague institute is “under control.” “We don’t think so,” Trump said. “We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.” The US has escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday. “We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.” “It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” Nonetheless, Trump said Russia is “very sophisticated, very smart, and they’re saying it’s very much under control,” even as he allowed that Russian officials had not disclosed much so far.

articles.title: Sunderland's National Glass Centre demolition plan faces scrutiny
articles.summary: Sunderland City Council's cabinet starts a process of restricting rights to knock down the building.
articles.body:
Plans to save the National Glass Centre (NGC) have inched forward with the local council backing a move which could eventually force the building's owner to seek planning permission to demolish it.

Sunderland City Council's Reform-led cabinet issued an Article 4 direction which it said "paves the way for further consideration" of the University of Sunderland's wish to knock down the centre.

The next stage will see notice served on the university and a period of 21 days for "third parties to make representations" ahead of a final decision in December on whether to implement planning requirements.

The university has been approached for comment.

The authority said interested parties, including the university, could give their views on the Article 4 direction in the coming weeks.

It would then review these comments and expected to make its final decision before the end of the year, however the protection would still only come into force following a 12-month notification period.

The council's cabinet said it had decided against issuing an immediate Article 4 direction to "protect taxpayers" from what it claimed could be exposure to "significant financial risk".

In a statement confirming the move, the authority said: "The decision taken by cabinet today will effectively remove the University of Sunderland's permitted development right to demolish the building in 12 months' time and means that, once it comes into effect, it requires a formal planning application to be submitted."

The council's leader Chris Eynon said: "The challenges the university faces in sustaining this building are well understood.

"The strength of feeling of those who wish to find a way of preserving the centre is equally clear."

The authority said it had decided to list the NGC as an Asset of Community Value following an application by the Save the Glass Centre campaign group.

This status makes it easier for local groups to bid for the building if it was ever put up for sale.

Eynon said the council had created a "window of opportunity" for all parties to consider their next steps.

articles.title: US Supreme Court hears challenge to air force UXO detonations in Guam
articles.summary: Advocacy group claims military sidestepped impact review, says case highlights lack of representation in US territories.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has begun hearing arguments in a case that could determine whether the US air force can continue to use a beach in Guam to detonate unexploded ordnance.

Wednesday’s hearing stems from a challenge by a Guam conservation group, Prutehi Guahan, which argues that the longstanding use of Tarague Beach to dispose of munitions may harm the ecosystem, damage an important cultural and historical site, and threaten the island’s water resources.

The case has gained attention for raising broader questions over the rights of residents of US territories, who cannot vote in presidential elections and have limited representation in the US legislature.

Guam became a US territory in 1898, in the wake of the Spanish-American Civil War. It has also served as a key US military hub in the western Pacific, hosting both Andersen Air Force Base and US Naval Base Guam.

The island has an estimated population of about 170,000.

The case before the Supreme Court hinges on whether the US air force followed proper environmental procedures before applying for a new permit to continue to dispose of and destroy hazardous munitions – including bombs, landmines and missiles – at Tarague Beach.

The air force has used the beach for the detonations since 1982 and applied for a permit to continue in 2021. Guam’s Environmental Protection Agency did not “deny or approve” the permit, and detonations have continued.

At the centre of Prutehi Guahan’s challenge is whether the air force followed the law.

In applying for the permit, the air force adhered to the 1976 Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which requires environmental regulators in US states and territories to regulate hazardous waste disposal.

Prutehi Guahan has also maintained that the air force must adhere to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, which requires federal agencies to conduct environmental impact assessments, including receiving community input, before undertaking major decisions.

In court filings, Prutehi Guahan, which means Protect Guam in the Chamorro language, said the air force disposal range is located “on ancestral land that the military seized from local families after World War II”.

It added the beach is “adjacent to culturally significant fishing locations – upon which local families depend for sustenance – and contains sites for collecting traditional medicines”. The area is one of the oldest occupied sites in the region, with archaeological evidence dating back to the 2nd millennium BC, Prutehi Guahan noted.

Prutehi Guahan also said the detonation site sits “above an aquifer that provides drinking water to over 80% of the island’s population”.

The court filing detailed studies that found munition disposal and detonation can send fragments into the surrounding ocean and reef, while releasing toxic chemicals.

Government lawyers have maintained that the air force followed environmental review procedures under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, arguing the process “displaces” any requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act.

They have further argued that, because the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in Guam has not issued a final determination on the 2021 permit, the challenge from Prutehi Guahan was premature.

A US district judge initially sided with the air force and threw out the case after Prutehi Guahan filed its challenge in January 2022. The US Court of Appeals’ Ninth Circuit, the country’s largest federal court, later determined the case could move forward.

The air force then appealed to the US Supreme Court.

Prutehi Guahan has underscored the significance of public feedback, which is required as part of environmental assessments under the National Environmental Policy Act.

In its filing, it pointed to a history of US government decisions about Guam made without input from residents, as well as a legacy of environmental damage. That includes two designated heavily polluted Superfund cleanup sites linked to navy and air force hazardous waste dumping.

“Decisions the military made nearly a century ago caused damage that still requires extensive and expensive cleanup,” the filing said. “And military decisions made more recently compound the damage Guam already bears”.

Writing for the SCOTUSblog which covers the US Supreme Court, Right to Democracy co-founders Neil Weare and Adi Martinez Roman said the case underscores the “unbalanced political relationship” between residents of US territories and the federal government.

“The people of Guam have little power or agency to influence federal decisions that impact their lives – which makes community consultation through federal laws like NEPA [National Environmental Policy Act] all the more important,” they wrote.

articles.title: Turning Point USA turns the tables on 'Saturday Night Live' after late-night sketch mocks campus recruiters
articles.summary: Turning Point USA called the "Saturday Night Live" sketch a compliment, saying the joke proves the organization has permeated popular culture.
articles.body: Conservative group Turning Point USA is laughing off a jab from "Saturday Night Live," calling the late-night satire a sign that the organization has entered mainstream pop culture. During Saturday’s episode, a sketch mocked a character’s hairstyle by comparing him to a "campus recruiter for Turning Point USA." The sketch featured members of the show’s cast and guest host Dakota Johnson, who played the main character. In a statement to Fox News Digital, TPUSA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet praised the joke, saying the organization took the shoutout as a compliment to its expanding national reach. COLORADO TPUSA CHAPTER ENROLLMENT 'FLAT' AFTER ELDERLY SUPPORTER WAS STRICKEN BY STUDENT WITH TACO BELL CUP "We saw the skit. We thought it was actually pretty funny and a testament to how the organization has permeated popular culture," Kolvet said, adding, "And, for the record, we thought his hair looked great." The sketch focused on men wanting a "scary mean girlfriend," played by Johnson, who degrades them and speaks her mind. "Has this ever happened to you? Your nice, supportive girlfriend won't give you a straight answer, and you're left wondering how she really feels? Well, not anymore. Introducing 'Mean Scary Girlfriend,'" a narrator says in the sketch. JON STEWART ASKS WHETHER 'THE DAILY SHOW' IS LIKE HIGH-SUGAR FOOD GIVING US 'POLITICAL DIABETES' The skit gained traction online, racking up over 2.1 million views on YouTube and 1.1 million views on X. Other jabs made by the "scary mean girlfriend" besides the Turning Point USA comment included "Oh good, you look like a pedophile on vacation" when one actor came out wearing a patterned shirt. The TPUSA comment was one of several jokes made at conservatives’ expense during the episode, including a sketch about guns tailored for women, several jokes about Trump Cabinet members during "Weekend Update" and a cold open centered entirely on Republican leaders. INSIDE THE HOUSE GOP'S 4-WEEK BATTLE PLAN TO SAVE ITS MAJORITY The Oct. 3 episode opened in the offices of the Republican National Committee, where officials were setting up to record ads ahead of the November midterm elections, which they said were looking "bleak." The cold open featured an impersonation of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, played by cast member Marcello Hernández, offering a message to Latino voters. It then showed a portrayal of Sen. Mitch McConnell, who appeared confused and unable to speak. The real McConnell recently returned to the Senate last month after a lengthy hospital stay from a fall at his home and a battle with pneumonia. Colin Jost also portrayed Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, with the character making the religious quip, "I'm putting God back in war, and it's working. Our soldiers are praying a lot more than they used to. I'm always hearing them say, 'Dear God, why?'" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It also featured characterizations of Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump, whom the show has frequently featured in its cold opens since Trump's return to the White House. An analysis by the Media Research Center’s NewsBusters, provided exclusively to the New York Post, found 91% of "Weekend Update" jokes targeted conservatives last season. Trump was the show’s most frequent target, accounting for more than 100 punchlines.

articles.title: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says
articles.summary: Moroccan, Algerian women killed in Abha, Sudanese national killed in Riyadh.
articles.body:
Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation.

Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The attack on Abha international airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, the Saudi General Authority reported.

The attack on King Khalid international airport, which is home to Saudi F‑15 and Typhoon fighter jets , in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said it is working, “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities”, to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.

On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.

A day later, at least one explosion was heard near the airport on September 19 in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid international airport.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swath of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait which connects the Arabian and Red Seas.

Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

articles.title: Witnesses spot Eritrean troops inside northern Ethiopia as tensions flare
articles.summary: Eritrea dismisses allegation as Ethiopia’s pretext for more war.
articles.body:
Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving through a northern town inside Ethiopia, witnesses tell the Reuters news agency, days after the neighbouring countries severed ties.

At least two witnesses told Reuters they saw “dozens” of Eritrean soldiers drive through Adigrat in two trucks on Wednesday. The town is located 25km (15 miles) south of the border with Eritrea.

The witnesses said they could identify the soldiers as Eritrean by their off-white camouflage uniforms.

Another Adigrat resident who was not in town at the time said family members had told him they had also seen Eritrean troops, according to Reuters, which could not independently verify their accounts.

“The Eritrean army has entered Tigray in uniform, equipped with heavy weaponry,” said Gebreigziabher Beyene, commander of the Tigray Peace Force, a pro-government militia that has fought alongside the federal army.

“This force is being struck by drones,” he said, adding Eritrea was “deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea”.

Last week, the chief administrator in Ethiopia’s northeastern Afar region said Eritrean troops were fighting in the area, but Reuters was unable to confirm the claim.

In a statement on X, Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Meskel did not deny that troops had crossed the border, but said Ethiopia’s government was creating “a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense’ to rationalise and camouflage its war of aggression”.

If confirmed, it would mark the first time Eritrean forces have been seen inside Ethiopia since the renewal of fighting between Ethiopian forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), on September 23.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, as well as Egypt and Sudan of backing the armed alliance which is fighting to remove the government. All three countries have denied involvement.

Eritrea announced it was severing ties with Ethiopia on Thursday after Addis Ababa announced it would close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats.

In a statement, Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Ethiopia’s actions had left it with “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.

On Monday, Ethiopian forces captured Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle, days after the TPLF confirmed that it had withdrawn from the city and moved its regional administration “temporarily” to another location.

It happened as Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five-year term , during which he insisted that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea.

On the same day, Eritrea joined Somalia, Sudan and Egypt in issuing a joint declaration calling for a political and peaceful solution to the war in Ethiopia.

The declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours.

articles.title: Trump says he does not think suspected Russian plague cases are a bioweapon
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday he does not think the suspected Russian plague cases are a bioweapon. “We don’t think so,” the president said in the Oval Office. He said Russia has said it has it “under control.” “They’re sharing it a little bit with our people,” Trump said. “I expect them to share it a…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he does not think the suspected Russian plague cases are a bioweapon.

“We don’t think so,” the president said in the Oval Office.

He said Russia has said it has it “under control.”

“They’re sharing it a little bit with our people,” Trump said. “I expect them to share it a lot with our people.”

A source familiar told The Hill’s partner network NewsNation that the U.S. has sent a formal diplomatic complaint to the Russian government demanding more information regarding the death of a woman working at the anti-plague research facility in Siberia.

A State Department official told NewsNation, “We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.”

Officials have said they’re monitoring the suspected pneumonic plague case in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia.

NBC News reported Monday that some 200 people were under medical observation in Siberia after a 28-year-old lab worker, who was possibly exposed to the pneumonic plague, died.

Pneumonic plague “is a rare and often fatal disease that can be transmitted by respiratory droplets from animals or persons infected with Yersinia pestis bacteria,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is different from pneumonia, which is the term for inflammation of the lungs.

On Sunday, the Russian consumer welfare service said the 28-year-old, who worked at an institute combating the plague in Irkutsk, died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” the outlet reported.

Trump said Monday the U.S. will “help” Russia with the potential outbreak.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump told reporters. “It’s a rough disease. We used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter.”

“The germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore,” he said.
