articles.title: Ultra-Orthodox rabbi’s anti-Zionist remarks stir Israel election row
articles.summary: Rabbi Dov Lando’s comments expose tensions over Zionism, conscription and Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox allies.
articles.body:
Comments by one of Israel’s most senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis postulating that Jews may have been better off without a state have prompted controversy in the country.

In footage broadcast by Channel 12 on Monday, the 96-year-old Rabbi Dov Lando, the spiritual leader of the Degel HaTorah party, also said that soldiers adhering to “Religious Zionism” killed in Israel’s wars were dying because of what their rabbis had taught them. The remarks, made at a closed meeting at his home in Bnei Brak, have set off a political storm three weeks before Israel’s October 27 parliamentary election.

“They are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah,” Lando said, adding that many military operations are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.

Lando’s comment came in response to a question about admiration among some ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – who have traditionally refused the military draft – for religious Zionists who combine Torah study with military service.

His comments aren’t new – they were first published in February 2025. However, their reemergence this week comes amid an election campaign in which ultra-Orthodox military service has become one of the sharpest fault lines in Israeli politics.

The Israeli Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that there was no legal basis for ultra-Orthodox seminary students to have exemptions from military service , and the government has since not been able to pass legislation restoring the exemptions. The issue has led to large protests on both sides of the divide.

“The question is not what he said, but why this discourse has been placed at the heart of the Israeli debate three weeks before the election,” Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera.

Lando’s party is one of the two factions of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which won seven seats during the last election in 2022, and had been part of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government before its ministers resigned last year.

The bloc did continue to intermittently support the coalition government, however, and Netanyahu has been wary of removing the military exemption – despite widespread opposition to it from many in Israel – out of fear that the UTJ and similar parties would remove their support completely.

Along with his role within Degel HaTorah, Lando is also one of the spiritual leaders of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community , which makes up roughly a third of the country’s estimated 1.45 million ultra-Orthodox Jews, also known as Haredim.

In May, he said he no longer trusted Netanyahu and called for parliament to be dissolved.

In the footage, he goes further. “It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” he says, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation”.

Zionism, he argues, “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual disaster on the Jewish people. He describes secular Israelis as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.

The comments reflect non-Zionist and anti-Zionist positions that used to be dominant within ultra-Orthodox Judaism, but take on an overt reference to the possibility of living within a non-Zionist state, something that is even more controversial in Israel.

Ibrahim Khatib, a conflict studies scholar at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said Lando’s remarks drew a line between Zionism and Judaism “from inside the Jewish community itself”, at a time when the official Israeli establishment “tries to bind them together”.

They also put to the test the narrative that Jewish communities in Arab societies were in danger and threatened, and that the Zionist movement came to “save them” at the formation of the state of Israel in 1948, he told Al Jazeera. However, Khatib cautioned that the ultra-Orthodox polity in Israel “is right-wing, its leaders hold right-wing positions, and some of them have made clearly offensive statements about Arabs and Palestinians”.

Israeli opposition leaders moved quickly after the footage of Lando emerged this week, taking it as an opportunity to attack a figure from a party within Netanyahu’s electoral bloc.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – one of Netanyahu’s main challengers in the upcoming elections – called the remarks “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist and anti-[Israeli military]”, but aimed his fire at Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who he said “back [Lando] and funnel tens of billions of shekels to him and his friends”.

Gadi Eisenkot, another opposition leader whose Yashar party has campaigned on enforcing the military draft, urged every Zionist party to pledge not to sit with Lando’s party.

Netanyahu, who publicly rejected Lando’s remarks in July when the rabbi accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support of the drafting of religious seminary students to the military, has not yet commented.

Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, put it bluntly: “Netanyahu is silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government.”

Jabareen sees Netanyahu’s silence as “calculated”.

“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim he needs to form a government,” he said. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”

The military draft of the ultra-Orthodox, Jabareen added, has turned “from an old dispute over religion and state into a question about the Israeli [social] contract itself: Who fights? Who dies? And who gets the exemptions, the budgets and the political influence in return?”

Mohammad Abu Rumman, an academic adviser at the Politics and Society Institute in Amman, said the significance of Lando’s remarks lay in the question that prompted them. The example of a young religious man who combines Torah study with military service, he said, “raises a question inside the ultra-Orthodox world itself: Why don’t we do the same?”

“When Lando describes their teaching as a distorted Torah, he is trying to close the door on emulating them,” Abu Rumman told Al Jazeera. “His words are aimed at his own audience as much as at his opponents.”

But Jabareen argued that the row exposes a rift more dangerous for Netanyahu than the familiar clash between secular and religious Israelis, because it runs through the right itself. Religious Zionists have paid a heavy human price in the war, while the ultra-Orthodox leadership still rejects conscription. Caught between those who pay the price of war and those who refuse to, Netanyahu needs both, and cannot satisfy them at once.

Whether the outrage over Lando’s comments translates into votes is less clear. Abu Rumman expects the remarks to “reinforce existing positions more than change voters’ choices”. The space where they could matter, he said, lies among right-wing voters who serve in the army and resent Netanyahu’s protection of ultra-Orthodox demands.

“If Netanyahu needs these parties to build a majority, that need will not disappear because of a rabbi’s remarks, however shocking,” Abu Rumman said. Netanyahu is also not the UTJ’s only suitor: Channel 12 reported that, frustrated by his failure to secure a law exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, the party would not rule out or oppose a government led by Eisenkot.

“The Israeli right has managed to bring under one political roof two currents with almost contradictory visions of the Jewish state,” Jabareen said. “One sanctifies the state and the expansion of its sovereignty. In the other, one of its most important rabbis can say it might have been better had the state never been founded.”

articles.body: A tree in New York’s Prospect Park has a history that began with a chance mutation in Scotland nearly two centuries ago. The Camperdown Elm was planted in the park in 1872 after Brooklyn florist A.G. Burgess donated it to the city. Its unusual ‘weeping’ branches gave it a distinctive appearance, but years of neglect eventually left the tree damaged.The tree’s story drew wider attention in 1967, when Brooklyn poet Marianne Moore wrote a poem about it and drew attention to its poor condition. Moore’s campaign soon drew support from residents, who were also concerned about the condition of other threatened areas in the park. According to NYC Parks, the campaign eventually helped lead to the creation of the Prospect Park Alliance to ensure the effort to protect the park and its historic trees.How did the 19th-century Brooklyn elm get its unusual shapeThe Camperdown Elm traces its origins to the late 1830s, when an unusual branch was discovered at Camperdown House in Dundee, Scotland. The branch came from a Scots Elm and carried a natural mutation that gave it an unusual growth pattern. It was attached to the trunk of a normal Scots Elm, producing a tree with the ‘weeping’ branches that became its defining feature.The tree also had another notable trait. It was immune to Dutch Elm Disease, which devastated elm populations across North America during the last century. The Camperdown Elm eventually reached New York, where one specimen was planted in Prospect Park and later became known for its unusual appearance and its decline after years of neglect.Poet Marianne Moore helped protect the Camperdown ElmThe Camperdown Elm came to Prospect Park in 1872 after A.G. Burgess, a Brooklyn florist who regularly donated trees to New York City parks, gave the tree to the park. It was planted on a raised mound so its distinctive weeping branches could hang freely without touching the ground.For years, however, the tree received little care and gradually fell into poor condition. That changed in 1967, when Brooklyn resident and Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Marianne Moore wrote a poem about the damaged elm. Her attention to the tree helped bring its condition before a wider audience. articles.title: Evicted 87-year-old who became a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis has died
articles.summary: Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home sparked a government crisis in Spain, has died, the Madrid Tenants’ Union announced on Tuesday.
articles.body: Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home sparked a government crisis in Spain, has died, the Madrid Tenants’ Union announced on Tuesday. Known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, she died just weeks after hundreds of people turned up to her door trying to prevent her from being evicted from the home where she lived for more than 70 years. She was forcibly removed on a stretcher after the private investment company, which owns the building in Madrid’s upmarket Retito district, hiked her rent from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970) – an amount that was unaffordable for the pensioner. “We regret to announce that Maricarmen has passed away today. As you all know, she was evicted on September 23, and has remained in hospital ever since,” the union said Wednesday. Maricarmen’s eviction sparked a wave of nationwide demonstrations over Spain’s housing crisis, with protesters setting up a large encampment of hundreds of tents at Puerta del Sol in Madrid. The landlord was forced to backtrack and agreed to allow her to move back once she was released from the hospital. “Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” the union added on Wednesday. Last month, Maricarmen spoke to supporters via a video from the hospital and urged them to continue to fight for their homes. “Please fight,” she told supporters. “I send you all a very big hug and thank you for everything.” There was an outpouring of grief and anger among protesters following the news of Maricarmen’s death. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed his condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones, posting to X: “A hug also to all those who today feel this loss as our own. Rest in peace.” People at the encampment in Madrid lit candles and held a moment of silence followed by an applause and shouts of “Maricarmen lives, the fight continues” and “We are all Maricarmen.” Some could also be heard chanting, “It’s not a death, it’s murder.” A group of the protesters began marching towards the parliament, with heavy police presence and barriers erected in the area. The protests have been largely peaceful, except for a few clashes between the demonstrators and police. Madrid’s Tenants Union, which was among the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend. On Monday, Sánchez called ⁠an ​early ​election for late November in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests. The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two proposed laws aimed at tackling the housing crisis. Analysts now expect Sánchez to focus on housing in an effort to win over popular support. The Bank of Spain has warned that the country is short of some 700,000 homes. “We need to renew people’s support,” Sánchez said on Monday. “We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.” The conservative Popular Party, which opposed the proposed housing reforms, is leading in opinion polls. It argues that the crisis needs to be solved by building more homes rather than by regulation. Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo on Wednesday also conveyed his condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. “No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall,” he posted to X in what some saw as a veiled criticism of Sánchez. “In the face of a person’s death, only respect is in order.”

articles.title: Oceans connect, not divide nations, PM Modi says, calls for secure maritime order
articles.summary: Doubling down on India’s stand that sea lanes must not be turned into war zones and proposal to end conflict on Black Sea, PM Narendra Modi said oceans
articles.body: Doubling down on India’s stand that sea lanes must not be turned into war zones and proposal to end conflict on Black Sea, PM Narendra Modi said oceans don’t separate countries but these connect them while calling for a free, open, secure and rules-based maritime order.In a message that was read out at Great Oceans Dialogue in Delhi, PM said, “The oceans do not separate us, they connect us, because what happens in one part of the world can have an impact far beyond its shores...Our vision is a free, open, secure and rule-based maritime that brings greater peace, prosperity and progress for all.” Modi said India’s maritime vision extends across regions and oceans, and is built on “cooperation, trust, mutual respect and mutual benefit”.His remarks come amid efforts to push a maritime understanding between Russia and Ukraine to keep the Black Sea open for commercial shipping and prevent attacks on vessels and critical maritime infrastructure. India’s three-part ceasefire plan seeks to halt attacks on energy facilities and other critical infrastructure; continuous and unhindered movement of grain, crude oil, LNG and LPG through Black Sea ports; and a complete stop to attacks on commercial vessels, merchant ships, and maritime operations to safeguard seafarers and global supply chains.The emphasis on maritime freedom assumes significance as attacks and disruptions in the Black Sea have affected commercial shipping, ports and movement of agricultural commodities during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.Participating in a panel discussion, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan said that they don’t make any distinction between national security and national economic security. Swaminathan added that maritime security affects all nations as he stressed on the need for partnerships. The officer said that the vastness of oceans made cooperation, collaboration and resource-sharing is essential.He added all nations should maintain maritime domain awareness and share broad assessments of threats. Invoking PM’s SAGAR and MAHASAGAR formulations, Swaminathan said maritime threats are increasingly transregional because oceans are contiguous. Cooperation, therefore, must extend beyond individual regions, with regions working together for collective security and growth.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam
articles.summary: Craig Morris was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison at Northampton Crown Court.
articles.body:
A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Craig Morris, 43, and Jogesh Bhandari, 60, bought luxury cars, holidays and a new home after pretending they could supply millions of boxes of nitrile gloves in the US and Germany.

They were convicted of two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation as well as concealing and transferring criminal property at Leicester Crown Court in July.

On Wednesday, Morris received three years and nine months in prison. Jogesh, of Mitchell Drive, Loughborough, Leicestershire, will be sentenced later.

Jogesh told his counsel he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" after having a pacemaker fitted last week and was not able to travel to Northampton, where the sentencing hearing took place.

His wife, former pharmacist Meenakashi Bhandari, 58, also of Mitchell Drive, did attend the sentencing hearing.

She was found guilty of concealing and transferring criminal property. She was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity.

Judge William Harbage KC said there was "no medical evidence" to properly explain Jogesh's absence and said a bench warrant would be issued. He is expected to be sentenced on 16 October.

Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris, of Forest Drive in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, was "very much working for him".

He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE).

"In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud."

The court heard that Jogesh and Morris made fraudulent deals under a company called Banton.

"They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it," Bisgrove added.

The court heard they defrauded US company Med18 and German firm MedTech by sending contracts for equipment they did not have.

Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit to buy cars, luxury goods and property."

The court heard the Bhandaris also used the money to pay off family debt, while Morris bought a house, the court heard.

The value of money Jogesh obtained and kept in the course of the fraud was £1.75 million, and Meenakshi laundered money to the value of £960,000, the court heard.

Morris had been receiving regular £5,000 payments from Jogesh before the two men fell out at the end of 2021, the National Crime Agency (NCA) previously said.

The agency said Jogesh worked with Frank Labruzzo, an attorney in the Louisiana Attorney General's Office, who provided a fraudulent escrow service - a bank account which holds funds until pre-arranged conditions are met.

The court heard that Labruzzo and another person involved have been convicted and sentenced in the US.

Sentencing Morris and Meenakshi, Judge Harbage said the pandemic was a time when "all of us had to make sacrifices and pull together for the good of society as a whole".

He added: "There were a few people though who sought to exploit that to make money for themselves, motivated by greed.

"I'm satisfied Jogesh Bhandari and Craig Morris fall into that category."

articles.title: Rubio calls for new era of power between US, Europe, with ancient Greece as backdrop
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday called for a new era of U.S. and European power on the global stage in a major speech delivered in Athens, Greece, with a dramatic background provided by the ancient Acropolis and the setting Mediterranean sun. He said the U.S. and its allies stand at a crossroads of…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday called for a new era of U.S. and European power on the global stage in a major speech delivered in Athens, Greece, with a dramatic background provided by the ancient Acropolis and the setting Mediterranean sun.

He said the U.S. and its allies stand at a crossroads of “whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.”

Rubio’s weighty address in an imposing setting and focused on a clash of civilizations is sure to fuel speculation that he’s pursuing a 2028 presidential run — although he’s said he has no plans for that at the moment .

It served to rally Europe alongside the U.S. by urging allies to rise from a “long slumber” and meet the occasion.

But the remarks come at a time when President Trump has alienated the continent with a trade war, threats to NATO allies and his pursuit of a controversial war against Iran. Whipsaw diplomacy with China, plus military adventurism and pressure campaigns in the Western Hemisphere, have further strained ties between the U.S. and Europe.

“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” Rubio said.

“This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim — reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization,” he continued.

“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.”

He touched on divisions among U.S. and European countries, pointing to the recent trilateral security agreement among the U.S., Denmark and Greenland that appeared to end Trump’s determination to take over the Arctic island, which is an autonomous territory of Denmark.

“We want to win together. We must win together.”

But Rubio’s speech also gave the secretary the opportunity to put his own messaging on the Make America Great Again culture and social wars against an impressive backdrop.

His address was a major production, The Washington Post reported , with staffers operating four State Department video cameras, including one mounted on a crane for cinematic shots of the secretary on Pnyx, a hillside in Athens that is viewed as one of the earliest assembly points for democratic traditions.

The secretary reached back to ancient Greek traditions of “contest, ambition, competition” and said “too much of the West has forgotten this quality,” criticizing reexaminations of U.S. and global history. He also denounced increased multilateralism, uncontrolled migration and third-country manufacturing, adding that the West collectively “allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.”

“And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together — understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them,” he said.

“And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.”

Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser, is viewed as one of the more palatable messengers in the Trump administration. Whereas European allies expressed shock and outrage at Vice President Vance’s 2025 Munich Security Conference address admonishing them for stifling free speech, Rubio received praise when he delivered remarks to the conference this year.

Rubio and Vance play down whether they are seeking the 2028 presidential nomination. But Rubio has outperformed Vance in hypothetical presidential match-ups with Democratic candidates and took a commanding lead over Vance in an August straw poll about the 2028 contest.

articles.title: Trump administration will have government lawyers representing unaccompanied immigrant children
articles.summary: The Trump administration cut ties with a nongovernmental organization that had managed 24,000 cases using a network of legal providers.
articles.body: MIAMI — The Trump administration is creating a team of attorneys to represent children who traveled alone to the United States in immigration proceedings, which critics say would deprive them of having lawyers who aren’t employed by the government and could put them at greater risk of deportation. The Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The decision, announced last week without fanfare, offered no details beyond that broad mandate. Health and Human Services said in a statement that its Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division will work under its general counsel’s direction toward “safely reuniting these children with their families and ensuring they have the legal support they need.” “This new division will give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families,” the department told The Associated Press in a brief statement. It didn’t answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational. The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008. It comes after the administration cut ties with the Acacia Center for Justice, a nongovernmental organization that managed 24,000 cases and held a contract to provide representation through a vast network of legal service providers. The change means migrant children will not have an independent representative to advocate for them who doesn’t have a conflict of interest, said Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center’s executive director. “Placing children’s legal representation and services inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,” Aber said. It “will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children’s rights and well-being.” Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that provides free legal representation and social services to unaccompanied children, called the creation of the new in-house HHS legal team “part of a pattern of attacks that this administration has engaged in, in terms of undermining zealous representation of unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.” The new division will work independently from other government agencies that deal with the minors, including the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for the custody and care of the children who arrive in the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian. There is some precedent for government-paid attorneys defending clients against government prosecutors in civilian and military courts, but as criminal defense lawyers and not in immigration court. But Young noted that the child’s lawyer, the judge and government attorneys seeking deportation will all be federal employees. Judges are appointed by the Justice Department, and prosecutors work at the Department of Homeland Security. “A government attorney who’s employed by the government most likely would be coached and encouraged to take the position of encouraging the child to agree to voluntary departure and to leave the United States rather than to present a full representation of the facts of their case,” Young said. Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates. Americans for Immigrant Justice, another nonprofit that provides free legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children, said it has been challenging to secure lawyers for the minors since the government suspended funding to legal aid organizations on July 31 through Acacia. Sui Chung, the group’s executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources. “To deny legal counsel to the most vulnerable among us — children who have already fled trauma — is a fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises,” Chung said. “Children deserve our strongest protection.” The government recently awarded a contract to another organization, Our Rescue, with a potential value of up to $244 million. The transition to Our Rescue, which has been challenged by Acacia, has led to short-term arrangements, including a temporary contract with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants.

articles.title: What happens next to Christa Pike?
articles.summary: Christa Pike is conscious after surviving a botched lethal injection, leading many to wonder if the state of Tennessee will try again to execute her.
articles.body:
The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory.

After state officials administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, Pike survived and was transported to a nearby hospital, where she was intubated. Six days later, her lawyers announced she was "conscious and speaking".

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and suspended all executions for the rest of the year.

The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area.

Doctor Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defence team, says he suspects the deadly chemical spread under her skin instead of her bloodstream, and, because of the the large dose, it could take days or even weeks for a clear picture of her health to emerge.

At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.

Pike's lawyers are seeking to have Pike's death sentence commuted to a lesser punishment of life in prison without parole. Lee, who has the power to pardon Pike or commute her sentence, has not indicated what the state will do in her case.

The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next.

Attempt to execute Pike by lethal injection again

The Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

"For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said.

Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol.

Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition.

Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure.

Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said.

Attempt to execute her with a different method

But Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method.

This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature.

Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means.

Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."

Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging".

Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws.

She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said.

Given Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there is a scenario where the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method.

It is also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained.

Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage.

Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment.

Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection.

That means it will likely take a while for any movement in Pike's case.

"At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Ross said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied.

Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered.

"If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said.

There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state.

The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed.

The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes.

articles.title: 'We'll do it': PM Modi gives slogan for 2047 goals; credits people’s support for 25-year unbroken run
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi chose the milestone of his unbroken run of 25 years as head of govt on Wednesday to deliver a message imbued with optimism and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi chose the milestone of his unbroken run of 25 years as head of govt on Wednesday to deliver a message imbued with optimism and passion for achieving the target of developed India by 2047, crediting people's support for his feat and asking citizens to join him in dedicating themselves to the ambitious goal."We will do it," Modi said at a BJP event, a clarion call which repeatedly punctuated his one-hour-long address and what, he said, has guided him in setting his goals, since he became Gujarat CM in 2001 with no administrative experience, and achieve them with support of "janshakti" (people's power)."Karma is my dharma. When I took oath as Gujarat CM, I never thought such an occasion will come," he said at Viksit Bharat Sankalp Sabha, asking people to take a pledge to put the nation first and not stop till India becomes a developed country. His speech came amid the opposition's high-decibel protest in the heart of the city over the SIR row but he appeared unfazed.Target unprecedented and extraordinary goals: ModiModi’s speech on his 25 years as head of govt came amid the opposition’s protest in Delhi over the SIR row, but he did not join the issue, except for a sideswipe at his rivals when he said a big tragedy for the country had been that it was divided for votes due to political expedience.Water crisis in agriculture or power shortage does not hit any particular caste or community, Modi said. “When a problem troubles everyone, then the solution too should cover everyone,” he said, adding this was why his govt linked good governance and saturation to inclusion.Reiteration of his “tireless” resolve to make India a leading player in a gamut of sectors, including tourism, education, sports, entertainment and science, ran through the nearly hour-long speech as its central theme.“Our pilot (Smit Machchhar) is being discussed globally today. Made-in-India planes will be discussed tomorrow... It will be an injustice to the country if we set small and easy goals. We should target unprecedented and extraordinary goals,” Modi said.“Viksit Bharat by 2047: we will do it. Top three economy: we will do it. Self-reliant: we will do it,” he said.Addressing the criticism that his target of “Viksit Bharat by 2047” is too far into the future, he said the idea of an independent India two decades before 1947 had looked improbable. India has 140 crore citizens now as against less than 40 crore then and is much more capable, he said.Modi said the Indian economy was considered a “gone case” when he took office in 2014, and the picture had completely changed now.Lauding RSS volunteers and BJP members, he recalled his rise from a humble background, saying he was always driven by a desire to learn. “No incident was a waste for me. Those who helped me win taught me humility. Those who brought me down taught me to stand up. Those who opposed me taught me the power of democracy. Every crisis was a test of my patience,” he said.Modi said he was never driven by ambition but mission, adding he never intended to contest elections and was busy helping others fight polls as a senior organisational functionary in BJP before being asked to take over as Gujarat CM.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Black voters, Jewish Democrats in Michigan wary of voting for El-Sayed, say 'he's taking advantage'
articles.summary: Black voters and Jewish Democrats in Michigan expressed deep reluctance to support Abdul El-Sayed in the state's heated Democratic Senate primary.
articles.body: A group of Black voters and Jewish Democrats in Michigan both expressed reluctance to support Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in the state, during interviews on Monday. "We went to Michigan, and we spoke to four total groups of Democratic voters, but two groups of Democratic voters here, who supported Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Senate primary. And these are Wayne County Black voters and Oakland County Jewish Democrats," MS NOW's Elise Jordan said of the voter groups during a segment on "Morning Joe." The Jewish voters were very apprehensive about El-Sayed's stance on Israel. Some of the Black voters told MS NOW that he hasn't taken advantage of opportunities to help them understand who he is and argued that they weren't going to vote for him just because he is a Democrat. DEMOCRATS FACE ‘DO-OR-DIE’ SPLIT WITH KEY VOTING BLOC IN RAZOR-CLOSE SENATE RACE "I think he's taking advantage that we as Black people are Democratic, and he thinks we're going to vote for him anyway. And I'm like, no sir. I'm like, to put uncommitted down on that little circle and move on," one of the Black Michigan voters said. "If you go to Congress to represent me, I need you to talk about what's going on in this community," the voter added. One voter said Israel was very important to him, but also said he had a transgender daughter, which made him reluctant to support the Republican candidate in the Senate race, Mike Rogers. "I have a transgender daughter who is 30, and I'm Jewish, and Israel is incredibly important to me. But a vote for Mike Rogers is a vote for my kid being oppressed and her rights being taken away," one voter said. "When I got into this race, I did so with the best interest of every single Michigander — regardless of political affiliation or background — in mind. To the Michiganders who are lifelong Democrats, if you’re looking at your party’s nominee today and don’t think his hatefulness and divisiveness is representative of your values, you have a home with us. We’re grateful for the support from Democrats we’ve received thus far and look forward to fighting for ALL Michiganders in the U.S. Senate," Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement. El-Sayed's campaign did not return a request for comment. FOX NEWS POLL: A SENATE BATTLE LOOMS IN MICHIGAN One Michigan voter said that it felt like "Sophie's choice" choosing between El-Sayed and Rogers. "It's like Sophie's choice quite honestly. You know, I love some of the things he's talked about. I think it's a little idealistic and a little extreme, and I'm a little concerned. But, you know, my big block is, it just comes down to this whole thing with Israel," another voter said. A Fox News poll released on Sept. 30 found the race was tight, with El-Sayed with a slim 1-point edge against Rogers, 50-49%, among Michigan likely voters. Yet among registered voters, the preference is almost identical, 51% El-Sayed vs. 48% Rogers. That’s a reversal since August, when Rogers was ahead by 4 points among registered voters, 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%. El-Sayed has come under fire over his ties to Hasan Piker, the far-left streamer who has campaigned with the Senate candidate. Piker has argued that America is "Pound for pound" worse than al Qaeda, "as far as the number of deaths." Piker said, "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." JEWISH MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS ADMIT THEY WILL VOTE REPUBLICAN IF ABDUL EL-SAYED BECOMES NOMINEE Another Michigan voter said during the segment, "On one hand, I'm like, OK, well, the choice is clear, but then all of a sudden it's like, I can't vote for Abdul because, once again, he's going against something that's innately me." A Jewish Democratic voter revealed during the discussion that she might vote for Rogers because of her daughter. JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE She said, "My daughter goes to University of Detroit Mercy, she's in her second year of law school, and she has to hide being Jewish. And it's a hard thing to say. When Oct. 7 came, horrible for her, lots of tears. I may go to Mike Rogers. Sorry, guys." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The group told her not to apologize, and said she deserved to feel comfortable with whoever she voted for. Jordan also spoke about the race with a group of Michigan voters who expressed regret over their past support for President Donald Trump. Of the six voters who were certain of their choice, five said they would support El-Sayed over Rogers.

articles.title: Mom dies shielding baby in horrific 15-story Bronx fall as police hunt suspect: report
articles.summary: Angel Carrasco is wanted after Nathaly Ramirez, 23, was allegedly pushed from a 15th-floor Bronx balcony with her baby in a suspected domestic violence attack.
articles.body: A New York City mother and her baby were allegedly pushed from an apartment balcony in a deadly attack that left the woman dead and her infant daughter critically injured, police said, as detectives hunt a man wanted in connection with the case. The NYPD identified Angel Carrasco, 31, as the man detectives are seeking after Nathaly Ramirez, 23, and her 8-month-old daughter were found outside their Bronx apartment building early Tuesday. The pair fell from a 15th-floor balcony, according to FOX 5 NY, which reported that investigators were looking for Ramirez’s boyfriend or recent ex-boyfriend in a suspected domestic violence incident. GEORGIA COLLEGE STUDENT MIRACULOUSLY SURVIVES 8-STORY PLUNGE AFTER METAL BENCH BREAKS HER FALL Investigators believe Ramirez tightly embraced her daughter during the fall, likely cushioning the baby from the impact, ABC7 NY reported. Neighbors described hearing a desperate plea moments before the horrifying incident. "Please don’t do this!" Ramirez screamed, according to neighbors cited by FOX 5. Officers responded to a 911 call at approximately 3:38 a.m. Tuesday outside 2550 Olinville Ave., where they found Ramirez and her daughter with injuries indicating a fall from an elevated position, the NYPD told Fox News Digital. DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE "Further investigation determined that both individuals had been pushed from a balcony," the department said. Officers rushed the baby to a hospital in critical condition. Emergency medical personnel transported Ramirez to a hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Police identified Carrasco as wanted in connection with the incident in an update Wednesday and released an image of him. The department’s statement did not specify his relationship to Ramirez or announce any charges. Sources told FOX 5 that the couple had a history of domestic violence and that police had been called to the apartment multiple times. A woman who lives two doors down told the outlet she had heard yelling from the apartment on numerous occasions. MARYLAND DAD BLAMED 'SATAN' AFTER 2-MONTH-OLD DAUGHTER DIED FROM HORRIFIC HEAD TRAUMA A neighbor identified only as Mike recalled an incident in January involving a man trying to force his way into Ramirez’s apartment, ABC7 reported. "He was kicking the door down trying to get into the apartment," Mike told the station. Anyone with information about Carrasco’s whereabouts can call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS, or submit a tip online at crimestoppers.nypdonline.org.

articles.title: 'The world is standing with you': Christian leaders from 122 countries unite in Jerusalem for Oct 7
articles.summary: The Friends of Zion summit drew delegations from 122 countries to Jerusalem, where released hostages and bereaved families shared their stories.
articles.body: Christian community leaders and influencers from around the world gathered in Jerusalem Wednesday for an international memorial marking Oct. 7 as part of the Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit. The event also included Jewish leaders, released hostages, bereaved families, wounded Israelis, ambassadors and diplomatic representatives to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. "Oct. 7 is the worst day in Israel’s history, a day of hopelessness," Dr. Mike Evans, founder of the Friends of Zion Heritage Center in Jerusalem, told Fox News Digital. ON OCT 7, CHRISTIANS MUST REMEMBER AND STAND WITH ISRAEL "People talk a lot about the more than 1,200 people killed that day, but not enough about the more than 70,000 who lost their homes and loved ones. You have a nation going through unspeakable pain, not only because of Oct. 7, but also because of the feeling that they are alone and that the world has turned against them," Evans added. "What I’m sharing on Oct. 7 is this: ‘You’re wrong. The world is standing with you,’" he continued. "You see the faces, languages and songs of people from around the world united to comfort you and stand with you. It’s not political. It’s for the Jewish people: You are not alone. We’re with you. We love you." CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND Hosted by actor and influencer Nathaniel Buzolic and reporter Erin Molan, Wednesday’s event in the Israeli capital was broadcast live on dozens of television networks around the world. "When other minority or groups suffer, there tends to be some sort of acknowledgment of that suffering, but when it comes to Jewish suffering, particularly at the hands of radical Islamists, there is not only silence but also denial and an attempt to downgrade the atrocities we witnessed, and we really have witnessed atrocities not just on Oct. 7 but in the continuation of that," Buzolic told Fox News Digital. Buzolic said supporting Israel is a moral imperative given what he described as efforts to destroy the country. He argued that the hostility toward Israel is rooted in a radical Islamist ideology that rejects peace and coexistence not only with the Jewish state, but also with Western societies more broadly. Released hostages Agam Berger, Sagui Dekel-Chen, Bar Kupershtein and Evyatar David attended the event, along with Bar’s grandfather, Holocaust survivor Michael Kupershtein. Sylvan Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress Israel and a full partner in the event, also participated. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Earlier in the day, participants visited Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust remembrance center. The Friends of Zion Ambassador Summit is being held for the second consecutive year and brings together over 1,000 participants from 122 countries. "The alliance is very strong. The vast majority of Zionists in the world are not Jewish; they are Bible-believing Christians," Evans told Fox News Digital. "The Christian Zionists worldwide don’t necessarily agree on the politics, but they agree on the people. They are uniting with the people of Israel." The delegation includes many young people as part of an effort to reach a generation that Evans said had been "poisoned" by countries such as Qatar at universities, as well as by artificial intelligence. The summit, held in cooperation with Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, opened Tuesday with an event on Jerusalem’s Mount of Olives. Evans said the site, which is associated with Jesus and his ascension, holds particular significance for participants and serves as a symbol of their faith. Israel’s Special Envoy to the Christian World George Deek said he was proud of the sustained support Israel has received from Jewish and Christian communities abroad since Oct. 7, 2023. LOST CITY WHERE JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES HAS FINALLY BEEN IDENTIFIED, EXPERT SAYS "The arrival of Christian leaders carries a powerful message that Israel does not stand alone. They have come to bear witness, meet people whose lives were shattered on Oct. 7 and carry their stories back to communities around the world," Deek told Fox News Digital. Deek said the bond between Israel and the Christian world has been built on "truth, courage and sheer determination" to confront antisemitism and other forms of hatred wherever they arise. "This visit is a testament to the strength of the bond between Israel and Christian communities despite attempts by various groups, including paid actors and anti-Israel organizations, to drive a wedge between them," he added. Deek said the special relationship between Christians and Jews rests on three foundations: a shared biblical heritage; a commitment to ensuring Jews can live free from antisemitism and fear and the right of Christians in the Middle East and elsewhere to live without intimidation. "The future of the Jews in Israel and the future of Christians are connected because we have a shared history. We share the same historical land, the same values, kings and prophets, and we have to stand together, especially when it comes to this warfare against the soul of Christians, trying to drive them away from Israel," Deek told Fox News Digital. Influencer Oli London first visited Israel six weeks after the Oct. 7 attack, traveling to Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where residents were killed and kidnapped and homes were burned during the massacre. "I felt it was so important to come back to honor the memory of the victims, advocate for those still suffering from trauma, raise awareness of their suffering and take part in mass prayers," London told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "I think it’s also important to show Christians the holy sites in Israel. I’m visiting the Sea of Galilee, the Mount of Olives, the Garden Tomb and other biblical sites to encourage Christians to return because Israel has had a difficult time over the past few years," he continued. London also praised the resilience of the Jewish people and addressed rising antisemitism around the world since Oct. 7. "Sadly, many people are either staying silent or jumping on the bandwagon of the anti-Israel trend, fueling hatred and bringing out antisemitic views in many people. Jewish people need support and need to know they are loved and supported by so many Christians," he said. On Thursday, members of the delegation will visit the Nova music festival site, where one of the central massacres of Oct. 7 took place, and meet with released hostages Romi Gonen, Elkana Bohbot and Noa Argamani, who were abducted from the festival. On Friday, the delegation will visit the ancient site of Shiloh in Samaria for a special tour and prayer event. Hooman Khalili, who is participating in the summit, was born in Iran and has been an outspoken supporter of Israel. He said he has visited the country 17 times over 21 months to create "Woman, Life, Freedom" murals. "I was invited and saw it as an opportunity to share with American pastors the work I have been doing to show the world how Israel and the Jewish people support women and the people of Iran," he told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This is one of those opportunities to come and pray for the land and the State of Israel, connect with other Christians and people who share my beliefs and values."

articles.title: Assam CM Himanta Sarma says woman sent to Bangladesh safe, son counters CM
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Assam CM Himanta Biswa Sarma's claim that Mumtaz Begum, a 43-year-old woman who was sent to Bangladesh in June, is safe and in daily touch with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Assam CM Himanta Biswa Sarma's claim that Mumtaz Begum, a 43-year-old woman who was sent to Bangladesh in June, is safe and in daily touch with her son has left her family with questions.Her son, Momruz Ali (26), told TOI Wednesday that he has had no contact with his mother and received no official communication from authorities about her whereabouts. "The CM says he knows she is safe... but we have no way to find out," he said. "We are just an ordinary family with little means. How will we ever find her?"Ali's plea to the Assam and Indian govts is simple: find his mother - "in Assam, India or Bangladesh". If she is alive, he said, "she has to be on either side". "It's govt's job. Assam Police must take responsibility for finding her," he said.The family's anguish is sharpened by Sarma's earlier remarks that people pushed across the border can cross back into India. "The CM, in a press conference two years ago, said that people cross over and return. In that case, they should search in Assam also. Why only Bangladesh?" Ali saidOn Sept 3, Gauhati HC directed the external affairs ministry to locate Mumtaz in Bangladesh and bring her back to pursue her case before the foreigners tribunal. It ordered Rs 2 lakh interim compensation for her husband, noting she had been expelled without an adult family member being informed.Declared a foreigner in 2019, Mumtaz had got relief from the HC in April this year, which set aside the tribunal's opinion and ordered fresh consideration of her case, citing deficiencies in its assessment of voter-list records and other citizenship documents. She appeared before the tribunal on May 30, was taken into custody and handed over to BSF before being sent to Bangladesh.TOI reported on Sept 29 that Bangladesh's home ministry had begun searching for Mumtaz after the newspaper reached out to authorities in that country. The matter was referred to relevant departments, but officials had no information. Searches in Sylhet have produced no breakthrough, with Sylhet Ran-ge DIG Mohammad Jahangir Hossain telling TOI he too was trying to locate her.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Federal appeals judges don’t reveal how they’ll rule on Saudi Arabia’s effort to end 9/11 litigation
articles.summary: Family members of victims of the Sept. 11 attacks packed a federal appeals courtroom in New York City on Wednesday.
articles.body: Family members of victims of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks packed a federal appeals courtroom in New York City on Wednesday as three judges heard arguments over whether legal claims against Saudi Arabia can proceed. The judges revealed through their questions that there are still many legal issues to be decided in the lawsuit even though it has dragged on for almost a quarter-century. They didn’t say when they might rule on whether claims can proceed to trial alleging that Saudi Arabia provided aid to at least two of the 19 men who hijacked planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field that day. Still, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada was killed in the attacks, said she was encouraged that more than 100 family members of 9/11 victims turned out and by the judges’ questions. “It really was a good day for us,” she said afterward. “The judges asked really meaningful questions and hammered the Saudi attorneys and didn’t let up. They weren’t buying what the Saudis were selling.” In lawsuits, hundreds of victims’ relatives and injured survivors, along with insurance companies and businesses, claim that employees of the Saudi government directly and knowingly assisted the hijackers and other plotters and fueled al-Qaida’s development into a terrorist organization by funding charities that supported them. Some defendants, including Iran, the Taliban and al-Qaida, already have been found in default. On Wednesday, lawyers from both sides were questioned repeatedly by the appeals judges who seemed unsure exactly how they would respond to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s claims that it should be dismissed as a defendant on sovereign immunity grounds. Lawyers for Saudi Arabia say the nation and the U.S. were partners in the 1990s against terrorism, al-Qaida and its founder, Osama bin Laden. Although 15 of the 19 attackers on 9/11 were Saudis, the Saudi government has long denied any involvement in the attacks. Lawyers for victims’ relatives claim that a group of extremist religious leaders in Saudi Arabia aided the hijackers. The appeal by Saudi Arabia stemmed from an August 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge George B. Daniels, who decided that the case could proceed in federal court, though he did not rule on the merits of the claims.

articles.title: 'I won Gladiators - now I'd love to become one'
articles.summary: Josh McDonald  won the third season of the hit TV programme, which aired earlier this year.
articles.body:
Having been bashed, bumped and bruised on his way to winning Gladiators earlier this year, you might expect Josh McDonald wants to put his feet up.

But the Glasgow fitness coach has not only signed up for another go on the famous Eliminator challenge - he fancies becoming one of the Lycra-clad stars.

The 29-year-old triumphed in the third season of the popular programme , which was filmed in Sheffield last year.

He is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall as part of a live tour across the country.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Several new Gladiators have joined the show for the new season, including three-time World's Strongest Man champion Tom Stoltman.

And Josh admitted he wouldn't mind "turning to the dark side" and joining the likes of Viper, Legend and Scotland's own Sabre .

He said: "I'd love to be a Gladiator and I think I'd be fantastic at it, with the message I bring, the personality I've got and the athletic ability I have.

"The problem is that while the gladiators are the pinnacle, they can't actually win the show - only the contenders can do that, and I'm really competitive.

"So you're better off being a contender than a Gladiator in some ways, as I don't think you would get the emotional rollercoaster that a contender will get from it.

"But if the opportunity to be a Gladiator came up, then I'd be there."

Josh was actually edged out in the first round of the show, but returned in the next stage after an injury to another contestant .

He did not let his second chance slip away, storming through to the final and taking the trophy after beating Tyler Spence, a teacher from Wigan, in a closely-fought contest.

However while Josh was jubilant to win the competition, the victory also brought with it a mixture of emotions.

He first watched the show growing up alongside his mother Clare, a single parent who raised him and his two younger brothers.

But in 2024, a few months before he got the offer to appear on the programme, his mother died after a long illness.

Josh then became the guardian of his younger brother Max, who was 14 at the time.

"I used to watch the show growing up with my mum," he recalls.

"She loved Wolf [from the 90s version] and it was something you'd sit on the couch going 'oh I could do that, I'd love that' and then the opportunity came up.

"Just before the show [was filmed] I wasn't taking care of myself as much, as I had lost my mum and was taking guardianship of Max and having that extra responsibility.

"There was a motivation of trying to prove myself that I could still compete and give Max something to cheer about, so I got back in training again."

Now he is trying to get ready for the games again, this time for the live tour.

It starts in Aberdeen this weekend and includes four shows in front of a home Glasgow crowd later this month.

"You can't go into a gym and just practice Duel, so what I am trying to do just now is focus on staying fit and healthy in general," he says.

"I've been at the local climbing centre trying to prepare for the Wall as that was the game I struggled with the most.

"In training I had been one of the quickest, and I'd thought to myself 'oh I'll get 10 points here' and then I messed it up every single time.

"I don't know if it was the pressure that got to me, as it's different when you have a Gladiator behind you, or maybe I just had too high expectations.

"I'm determined to do better on the tour."

Getting back involved with Gladiators was not something Josh - who proudly displays the trophy from the show on a table in his living room - had to think twice about.

"I'd have Gladiators champion tattooed on my forehead if I could so I bit their hand off to do it," he said.

"Doing the TV show was one of the highlights of my entire life and something I'll never forget so having the opportunity to relive it in Scotland is so exciting."

But no matter what is thrown at him Josh said being a guardian to Max was the toughest challenge he faced in life.

He added: "I've always had big brother responsibilities, and my mum was a single parent so I always tried to support her.

"But as soon as I stepped into the guardian role it flipped everything on its head. It's not something you can prepare for."

Since winning Gladiators he has become involved in various charities, including raising awareness for kinship charities .

Josh hopes he can help highlight that there is support available for people in similar situations to himself.

He said: "I thought I was one in a million and I had to stumble my way through it.

"A lot of the information I obtained was just me sourcing it and I felt very isolated.

"But there are thousands of us out there and I want them to feel like they are not alone."

articles.title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.summary: Lawyers say the convicted killer was surprised to have survived and remained "shackled" to her hospital bed.
articles.body:
A lawyer for convicted murderer Christa Pike says that she woke up in hospital "angry and confused" after she survived a botched execution attempt last week.

Her first words were to ask "Where am I?" and "Who are you?", her lawyer Randy Spivey recalled during a news conference.

Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee.

Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented, and that no other US inmate has survived a lethal injection from executioners.

A court on Wednesday ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.

Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care and is being restrained at her hands and feet in her hospital bed, her lawyers said at the news conference after a court hearing on Wednesday.

Spivey said that her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.

However, in a "shock to everyone", she began to talk on Tuesday, while recalling only limited details about the execution attempt.

Pike, he said, had helped the execution team find a vein in her arm, and she was kind and polite while she was being injected.

Then she woke up in a hospital with a tube down her throat and people she didn't know. Both of her arms, he said, are now "tremendously swollen".

"We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said, noting how she was left "angry and confused" by the ordeal.

He added that she also has a blood clot in one of her arms, pneumonia, and is not able to swallow.

Pike is believed to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.

After it became clear Pike would not die, following two rounds of the drug pentobarbital, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.

Earlier on Wednesday, lawyers appeared before a judge for an emergency hearing, where her team requested that all evidence from the botched execution be preserved.

That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's lawyers, began by describing the "roadblocks" that have made it challenging to communicate with his client.

"Up until yesterday our client was unconscious, and unable to communicate," he told Judge Chancellor I'Ashea Myles. Pike is now "speaking limitedly", he said.

Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers called attention to the "unusual procedural position here", prompting agreement from the judge. He argued that an emergency motion was unnecessary because the state is already compelled to preserve evidence.

Still, Judge Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.

The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.

She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

Asked by the judge whether the state intended to reschedule execution for Pike, Ayers said he did not know the answer.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief said he is resigning after the failed execution.

Ihnen asked the judge to allow Pike access to a phone so she can call her lawyers, and they can have "continuous liberal access to Ms Pike". He said they were kept waiting for over two hours during a recent attempt to visit her in hospital.

Ihnen added that Tennessee prison officials are keeping her "shackled" to her hospital bed, despite requests from medical staff that the handcuffs be removed.

Her lawyer also requested that the Tennessee Department of Corrections be required to notify his team 48 hours before she is transferred from the hospital to any state hospital or other government-run facility.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.

articles.title: Deadly attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi airports highlight widening fallout from Yemen conflict
articles.summary: Saudi aviation authority says both Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have come under attack.
articles.body: Houthi rebels attacked two Saudi airports killing three people and injuring 36 others this week, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said Wednesday, as the conflict in Yemen increasingly spills across the border into the kingdom. In a statement, GACA said Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport came under attack on October 6 and 7. The attacks prompted a security alert from the US Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens of potential drone and missile attacks and cautioned that the conflict could escalate. “The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate,” the mission said Wednesday. “US citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.” The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015. The conflict flared up in July 2026, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unraveled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces. According to GACA, the attack on Abha International Airport on Tuesday killed two female residents, one Moroccan and one Algerian national, and wounded 28 others, including Saudi citizens as well as Bangladeshi and Filipino residents. A separate attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh on Wednesday killed a Sudanese resident and wounded eight people, including five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents and one Pakistani resident, the authority said. The Houthi-controlled armed forces claimed responsibility for both attacks. The group said it had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and claimed the strike disrupted air traffic in Riyadh. Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said Saudi forces had destroyed the ballistic missile launcher used in the attack on Riyadh. In a post on X, al-Maliki said the launcher was destroyed in Sanaa while preparations were underway for “another imminent attack against Saudi Arabia.” A day earlier, the Houthis said they had carried out a ballistic missile attack on Abha International Airport and similarly claimed it had disrupted airport operations. The group also renewed its warning to international airlines against operating flights through Saudi airspace, saying it had become “a theater for our military operations,” while excluding the airspace around the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment on the Houthi claims. The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press ahead with Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at rolling back recent gains made by the Iran-backed Houthis. The escalation has also prompted Saudi Arabia to strengthen defense cooperation with regional allies. Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to move forward with the implementation of collective defense measures under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance. In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan’s military confirmed to CNN on Wednesday that Pakistani forces are already stationed in Saudi Arabia as part of the alliance. Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security was “absolute” and described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense and deterrence. He added that the pact includes a NATO-style provision under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all. The United States has also increased its support for Saudi Arabia’s campaign. More than 100 US military advisers are currently in Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the kingdom’s military operations against the Iran-backed Houthis, CNN reported last month citing multiple sources familiar with the effort. The assistance comes as fighting intensifies on the Arabian Peninsula and raises concerns that the conflict could expand further, potentially threatening a second major maritime corridor in the Middle East in addition to the Red Sea. In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia. The strikes on airports in both southern Saudi Arabia and the capital underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign. With civilian infrastructure now coming under renewed attack, the hostilities are showing signs of expanding beyond the battlefield in Yemen and posing a growing challenge to Saudi security and transportation networks. The activation of the Mecca Alliance and confirmation that Pakistani forces are already deployed in the kingdom suggest Saudi Arabia and its allies are preparing for the possibility of a broader regional security confrontation.

articles.title: ‘No to the father, no to the son’: Thousands march in Rio against Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Students and other protesters marched against Flavio Bolsonaro after he advanced to Brazil’s presidential run-off.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have taken to the streets of Rio de Janeiro in a student-led protest against presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and the growing influence of Brazil’s far right.

The march happened on Wednesday, just days after far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, earned the most votes in the first round of the country’s presidential race.

Bolsonaro won 47 percent, ahead of his closest rival, incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who gained 45 percent support.

Since neither candidate surpassed the 50 percent threshold, they will face each other in a run-off on October 25.

The results have triggered fears that Brazil could become the latest Latin American country to see its presidency switch from left to right.

Protesters marched through downtown Rio carrying signs reading “Never again Bolsonaro” and “No to the father, no to the son”. Others held banners reading “Dictatorship never again” and “Get out Bolsonaro”.

“I’m here because I believe in democracy. Because I’m scared,” said Alice Carneiro, 25, an administrator in maritime shipping who participated in the protests. She explained that, under a far-right government, she feared a backlash against her wife, who is transgender.

Jair Bolsonaro, the former president, led the country from 2019 to 2023. But his single-term tenure was marked by a series of controversies related to his far-right policies.

He voiced support for Brazil’s past military dictatorship, which was responsible for the disappearance and murder of hundreds of perceived dissidents. He also spread unfounded claims about the accuracy of Brazil’s election system, leading to a court ruling that barred him from holding office for eight years.

Currently, the former president is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of plotting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. After Lula’s inauguration in 2023, Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed government buildings in the capital, reportedly hoping to trigger a military uprising.

Critics have framed Jair Bolsonaro’s actions as a threat to Brazil’s democracy.

But Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has received his father’s endorsement, and he has backed amnesty for his father, a prospect that has raised concerns among protesters.

“I find this rise of the far right and the rise of Bolsonarism in Brazil very, very sad,” said Emmanuel Araujo, 19, who is preparing for university entrance exams.

“Lula might not be my preferred candidate,” Araujo added, “but amid this barbarism, we have to choose between someone we can keep criticising and someone who might take away our right to speak.”
