articles.title: The 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests in Spain dies
articles.summary: MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis, died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
articles.body: MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis, died on Wednesday while hospitalized. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal’s lawyer announced her death. Known widely as “Maricarmen,” she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain’s housing affordability crisis. “All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said in a post on X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.” The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain’s Parliament who chanted “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!” Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid. “A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it,” she said. “It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it, if there is any result from all that she has fought for, as well. That’s what angers me the most, honestly.” Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health. Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country. Maricarmen’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated. “Maricarmen’s case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” Duro said. She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment. “Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.” The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain’s government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so. Protesters camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death. Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment. After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital. “Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn’t asking for anything else,” Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. “She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.” Maricarmen’s plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain’s unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: “I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end.” Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences. “I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage,” the Popular Party leader wrote. “When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect.”

articles.title: Chicago demolished LeClaire Courts in 2011 and left much of its 32-acre site vacant; 15 years later, a $127 million first phase is set to bring 183 homes as part of a plan for up to 700 units
articles.summary: Fifteen years after the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the LeClaire Courts public housing complex, the 32-acre site is finally set to be reborn.
articles.body: Fifteen years after the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the LeClaire Courts public housing complex, the 32-acre site is finally set to be reborn. The Chicago City Council has approved a funding package for the first phase of redevelopment, a $127 million plan that will deliver 183 apartments across two six-story buildings on Cicero Avenue. The broader vision calls for as many as 700 residential units, most of them affordable, along with nearly 440,000 square feet of commercial space and publicly accessible open areas, according to reports by Urbanize Chicago and Chicago YIMBY.A long-vacant site near MidwayLeClaire Courts was a large public housing development completed in the 1950s on Chicago’s Southwest Side. The complex sat between Cicero Avenue and Lavergne Avenue, with 45th Street to the south and the Stevenson Expressway to the north, just minutes from Midway International Airport. By the time it was demolished in 2011, the site had become emblematic of the challenges facing mid-century public housing projects across the country.After demolition, much of the 32-acre parcel remained vacant for more than a decade. The empty lots bordered industrial areas, major roadways and airport infrastructure, creating a large but complicated development site. For years, the land stood as a reminder of a former neighbourhood that once housed thousands of residents but had not yet been replaced by a new community.The new plan aims to transform that vacant land into a mixed-income, mixed-use neighbourhood. The first phase will occupy the west side of Cicero Avenue between 44th and 45th streets, positioning the new buildings along a busy corridor with access to public transit and major highways. That location is seen as a key asset for connecting future residents to jobs, schools and services across the city, reported Chicago YIMBY.Two buildings, 183 homes and a childcare centreThe first phase consists of two six-story mixed-use buildings designed by architecture firm SCB. Together, they will offer 183 apartments in a mix of studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom floor plans. A central walkway and green park space will connect the buildings, with a 134-vehicle parking garage located behind them. The design includes surface parking, two playgrounds, landscaped gathering areas and accessible walking paths intended to link eventually to on-site retail and services. One of the buildings will house a 10,000-square-foot early childhood centre on the ground floor, providing childcare for residents and the surrounding community. The other building will include a community room and about 2,200 square feet of additional first-floor retail space. Those amenities are meant to support daily life for families and create a sense of community within the development, as per the reports.Residents will have access to on-site amenities such as a fitness centre in each building, multiple lounges, community rooms, resident services meeting space, laundry facilities, package rooms and bicycle storage. A rooftop apiary on the north building is planned to enhance urban biodiversity, provide fresh honey for residents and offer educational opportunities for families. Community-centered murals are also planned for both buildings.Affordability at the core of the planAround 90 percent of the 183 homes in Phase I will be designated as affordable through income and rent restrictions tied to the project’s public funding. The remainder will be available as market-rate apartments. Some of the affordable units will be reserved for households using Chicago Housing Authority vouchers, ensuring that former public housing residents and other low-income families can access the new homes.Chicago YIMBY reported that the affordability structure is supported by a complex stack of public and private financing. The City Council-approved funding package includes a $43.7 million senior construction loan, a $7 million permanent loan, $9.5 million in city multi-family program funds, $5.5 million in tax increment financing, a $24.5 million CHA loan, a $700,000 Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity grant proceeds loan, $33.7 million in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity, $1.25 million in Illinois Affordable Housing Tax Credit equity and a $1.2 million deferred developer fee.That layered financing reflects the reality of building affordable housing in Chicago. Projects that rely on multiple public sources must meet various compliance requirements, which can increase costs but also ensure long-term affordability. For residents, the result is a development where most units remain affordable for decades, rather than converting to market rate after a short period.A partnership to rebuild a neighbourhoodThe redevelopment is being led by a collaboration between Cabrera Capital Partners and The Habitat Company, working with the local office of SCB. Construction of the residential phase is being led by The George Sollitt Construction Company. Permits for the new construction have been filed, and work is expected to begin in late 2026, with a groundbreaking approved for this fall, as per reports.Habitat’s multi-phase plan envisions the full 32-acre site eventually holding up to 700 residential units, most of them affordable, along with significant commercial space and open areas. The first phase is just the beginning of that larger vision, which aims to create a complete neighbourhood rather than a single housing project. Future phases could add more homes, retail, healthcare facilities and other services to the site.For former residents and their families, the redevelopment carries emotional weight. Online comments on project coverage include messages from people who grew up in LeClaire Courts, expressing hope that they might one day return. Some note that the original complex functioned as a full neighbourhood, with churches, parks, daycare, after-school programs and small businesses, and they hope the new plan will honour that legacy while creating a modern, mixed-income community.From demolition to reconstructionThe 15-year gap between demolition and reconstruction highlights the challenges of redeveloping large public housing sites. Financing, planning, community input and market conditions all play a role in determining when and how a project moves forward. For LeClaire Courts, the combination of city funding, CHA support, tax credits and private investment has finally made the first phase viable.When completed, the new buildings will replace a long stretch of vacant land with homes, childcare space and retail. They will also reintroduce residents to a site that once supported a dense, working-class community. The hope is that the redevelopment will not only provide housing but also help revitalise the surrounding area, bringing new activity to Cicero Avenue and creating connections to nearby employment centres, including the airport and industrial parks.As construction begins, the project will be watched closely by housing advocates, city officials and neighbours. If successful, it could serve as a model for how large, formerly public housing sites can be transformed into mixed-income communities with deep affordability. For those who remember LeClaire Courts as a home, the new buildings represent a chance to see a familiar address become a living neighbourhood once again.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pro wrestler Karl Fredericks relishes opportunity to showcase who he truly is at Produce Wrestling's Skoden
articles.summary: Karl Fredricks opens up about his deep cultural identity struggles and why his Produce Wrestling match on Indigenous Peoples' Day means so much.
articles.body: Karl Fredricks still has something to prove. The 36-year-old Reno, Nevada, native has already made a name for himself. He was the 2019 Young Lion Cup winner in New Japan Pro-Wrestling, he won titles at All Pro Wrestling, appeared in WWE NXT as Eddy Thorpe and was named one of the best 500 singles wrestlers by Pro Wrestling Illustrated in 2021. But one of his most meaningful accomplishments will come Monday when he appears at Produce Wrestling by Orange Crush’s Skoden event at Roulette Intermedium in New York. Fredricks will be one of the wrestlers with Native American ancestry on the card as the show celebrates Indigenous Peoples’ Day. He will be taking on Javi in a singles match. He talked about the upcoming event with OutKick Dropkick and suggested he wanted to show he was more than what he described facetiously as being a "cartoon Indian." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE "I'm a damn pro wrestler, and that's what Karl Fredericks is. That's what this has always been about. It was my love for pro wrestling, my love for performing, what I learned in Japan, that fighting spirit, the true heart and soul of professional wrestling and going out there, b---s to the wall. Not for four minutes, 4-7 minutes at a time," he explained. "That's what TV wrestling is. That's just playing the character I was (as Eddy Thorpe) being, being what I felt like was a cartoon Indian at times and doing all that stuff. "Working for a company like Produce is a blessing to be. I'm blessed to be here with people that give me a platform to be myself, to wrestle my match, to wrestle my style." Fredericks opened up about growing up with a Native American background and being unable to see anyone on television or in movies that looked like him. He lamented films portraying Native Americans as the bad guys. He said that being able to open up and be true to himself inside and outside of the ring has helped him get to where he is now – and he’s heard about it. He said he’s received messages from those of a similar background who were happy to see him on TV regardless of the role he was playing or the type of character he was asked to portray on television. "I would get messages all the time, and they did so much for me … Just the fact that we got a guy. Regardless of how they, I'm sure they had opinions on, you know, the way things were, but like they were just happy to have a guy. And so, I knew at the same time it was like, it was just important to be there giving my best effort regardless of what I was doing and I believe I did that, and now it's just it's going back out into the world as myself with a point to prove, and that's on both ends cause like I've experienced this struggle with cultural identity." Fredericks described a deep pain he felt growing up because, to some of his Native friends, he was a "White boy," but when he would be with his White friends, he would be the "native friend." "There are days when I'm, again, in the spirit of being facetious, and then there's a lot of pain in the experience behind it where it's just like, man, maybe I am just a f---ing Indian, whatever that means, and I don't know what that even means, because that's also, that's still something that, you know what I mean? Like I would, I wouldn't call myself (that). I do for the sake of the situation, essentially. So, I think it really is just up to me." Fredericks recalled one instance in the WWE Performance Center where tapping into his true self showed he was on the right path. He said the wrestlers he was with on one particular day got a chance to do promo work in front of John Cena. He said he grabbed his choker, jewelry and dressed up before bolting to the facility. He ended up cutting a promo on Roman Reigns. "I cut a promo on Roman Reigns, calling himself ‘The Tribal Chief, because culturally that's not in their vernacular and he was heel at the time, so I remember saying things like, ‘Where I come from, the chief is the wise man.’ The chief's a protector or provider, like the all of these good things, so I call out, I do this promo and John had no notes, said he loved it, said he understood who I was from top to bottom." Fredericks said, later in the session, he essentially asked Cena how he could stand out in the ring where nobody who was watching looked like him and didn’t feel like he was supposed to be to others unless he was "covered in animal bones." Fredericks said Cena described his question as "beautiful" and it clicked to him that whatever he was doing in the ring and whatever he was trying to portray was solely up to him and him alone, including saying no to a hair vs. hair match idea. "The last year and a half has been very tough mentally, just processing a couple years of my life, as well. Didn't have too much time to really process the end of the New Japan run and now all of a sudden, I'm here and I'm Karl again, and it’s been a lot of that," he told OutKick Dropkick. "I'm really excited for this opportunity to celebrate the Indigenous Peoples' Day, help out some other homies, some kids that I've been either watching or know of or had asked around, … It's gonna be a good day. articles.title: Bank of England reveals the four animals to feature on banknotes
articles.summary: The decision comes after nearly half a million people cast their votes from a shortlist of 18 creatures.
articles.body:
Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.

The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.

The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.

Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.

"We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier.

A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations . Respondents were invited to select up to six.

More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes.

The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba).

The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category.

The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal.

The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline.

The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively .

Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes.

Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years.

He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch.

"We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said.

Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland .

Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history.

On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing.

The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do".

The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time.
